title: PeKa B40 (PeKa Sihat): who qualifies, free screening, benefits and how to check
desc: If you receive STR and are 40 or over, you can get a free health screening at a private GP clinic, plus help with medical devices and cancer treatment costs. Who qualifies for PeKa B40, how to check, what the screening includes, and the other schemes you may be entitled to.
headings: What is PeKa B40? · Who qualifies? (Kelayakan PeKa B40) · How to check your eligibility (Semakan PeKa B40) · The four PeKa B40 benefits · What the free health screening includes · mySalam: critical illness and hospital income · What happened to Skim Perubatan Madani? · PERKESO free health screening (for workers)
keywords: Guides PeKa B40 PeKa B40 Skim Peduli Kesihatan untuk Kumpulan B40 mySalam kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october kesihatan mental depression anxiety stress kemurungan klinik doctor doktor gp saringan check-up checkup medical
body: PeKa B40 is for Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR) recipients and their spouses aged 40 and above. There is no need to register: just bring your MyKad to a panel clinic. The free screening covers a check-up, blood tests for diabetes (HbA1c), cholesterol and kidney function, a urine test and a mental health check, with a second visit to go through the results. Other benefits: medical device aid of up to RM20,000, a RM1,000 incentive for completing cancer treatment, and help with transport costs. Check your eligibility at kelayakan.pekab40.com.my. The scheme is being renamed PeKa Sihat, with the same benefits. mySalam (critical illness and hospital income) continues in 2027. PERKESO offers separate free screening to contributors aged 40 to 59. PeKa B40 (Skim Peduli Kesihatan untuk Kumpulan B40) is a Ministry of Health scheme, run by ProtectHealth Corporation since April 2019, to help lower-income Malaysians catch diseases such as diabetes, high blood pressure and kidney disease early, and to ease the cost of treatment. On 16 October 2026, the government announced that PeKa B40 will be renamed PeKa Sihat . The benefits stay the same, and the Ministry of Health will announce the details. Budget 2027 allocates RM80 million to the scheme. The screening matters: of the 328,302 people screened in 2025, 44.5% had at least one health problem that hadn’t been detected before . You receive Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR) , or you are the registered spouse of an STR recipient, and you are a Malaysian aged 40 or above . You don’t need to apply or register separately. If you are eligible, you can go straight to a PeKa B40 panel clinic with your MyKad. Go to the official eligibility checker at kelayakan.pekab40.com.my . Enter your MyKad number. If you are eligible, find a panel clinic using the PeKa B40 provider search , or look for the PeKa sticker at your local clinic. Only use the official websites, and never pay anyone to “register” you for PeKa B40: the scheme is free and there is nothing to register for. Benefit What you get 1. Health screening A free check-up and tests at a panel clinic (details below) 2. Medical device aid Up to RM20,000 for devices in 10 categories. Applied for by a Ministry of Health specialist for patients treated at government hospitals, after you have done the screening 3. Cancer treatment completion incentive RM1,000 : RM300 when you start treatment and RM700 when you complete it 4. Transport incentive Up to RM500 in Peninsular Malaysia, or up to RM1,000 in Sabah, Sarawak and Labuan, for people receiving benefit 2 or 3 The screening takes two visits to the same clinic. You don’t need to fast. First visit: questions about your health and your family’s medical history, a mental health screening questionnaire, and a physical examination (including blood pressure and weight). Women may have a clinical breast examination, and men at risk a prostate check. Blood is taken for a full blood count, HbA1c (for diabetes), cholesterol and kidney function , plus a urine test. Second visit: the doctor goes through your results, gives advice, and refers you for treatment if anything needs follow-up. If your results show a problem, don’t ignore it. Diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol usually have no symptoms until they cause damage. See our guides to normal blood sugar and HbA1c levels and blood pressure and cholesterol . The PeKa B40 screening includes blood tests for diabetes, cholesterol and kidney function. mySalam is a separate free protection scheme for STR recipients and their spouses, up to age 65, run through a trust fund under the Ministry of Finance. The Budget 2027 speech confirmed it will continue in 2027. Up to RM8,000 , paid once, if you are diagnosed with one of 50 critical illnesses. RM50 a day in income replacement when you are admitted to a government hospital, for up to 14 days (RM700) a year. Help with medical devices of up to RM30,000. By the end of 2025, about 1.88 million people had received mySalam payouts, totalling RM1.42 billion. Check your status and how to claim on the official mySalam website . Skim Perubatan Madani (SPM) began in June 2023 and let STR recipients see a private GP for minor illnesses such as coughs, colds, diarrhoea and minor wounds, up to RM250 a year for a household, RM125 for a senior living alone and RM75 for a single adult. From February 2024 it ran in 10 districts only, including Kuala Lumpur, Petaling, Klang, Gombak and Hulu Langat. Its budget was halved to RM50 million for 2026, and the scheme was reportedly not funded in Budget 2027 . The Ministry of Health hasn’t issued a closure notice, so check ProtectHealth or MySejahtera for the latest before you go. Klinik Kesihatan remain the lowest-cost option for everyday illness. If you work and contribute to PERKESO (SOCSO), you may qualify for its free Health Screening Programme (HSP) , separate from PeKa B40: Who: Malaysian citizens aged 40 to 59 who are active contributors under the Invalidity Scheme, with at least 12 months of contributions. What: a physical examination, mental health screening, blood tests (including HbA1c, cholesterol, kidney and liver function), a urine test, and a Pap smear and mammogram for women. How: check your eligibility and book a panel clinic in PERKESO’s SEHATi app or portal. The results show why it matters: among workers screened from 2023 to 2025, about 19% had diabetes and more than 17% had high blood pressure. For other free options, see our guide to free health screening in Malaysia . Who is eligible for PeKa B40? Malaysians aged 40 and above who receive Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR), and their registered spouses aged 40 and above. There is no separate registration. How do I check if I qualify for PeKa B40? Enter your MyKad number on the official checker at kelayakan.pekab40.com.my. If eligible, bring your MyKad to a PeKa B40 panel clinic. Is the PeKa B40 health screening free? Yes. The screening, including blood and urine tests and the follow-up visit, is free for eligible people at panel clinics. Do I need to fast before the PeKa B40 screening? No. The blood tests used, including HbA1c for diabetes, don’t require fasting. What is PeKa Sihat? PeKa Sihat is the new name for PeKa B40, announced in October 2026. The benefits remain the same, and the Ministry of Health will announce further details. How much is the PeKa B40 medical device aid? Up to RM20,000 for devices in 10 categories, applied for by a Ministry of Health specialist for patients at government hospitals, after the person has done the PeKa B40 screening. Is mySalam still available? Yes. The Budget 2027 speech confirmed mySalam continues in 2027 for STR recipients and their spouses up to age 65, with up to RM8,000 for critical illness and RM50 a day for hospital stays. Who can get PERKESO’s free health screening? Malaysian PERKESO contributors aged 40 to 59 who are active under the Invalidity Scheme with at least 12 months of contributions. Check and book in the SEHATi app.

title: Normal blood sugar levels and HbA1c: charts, prediabetes and early signs of diabetes
desc: What is a normal blood sugar level, and what does your HbA1c result mean? Clear charts using Malaysia’s own guideline cut-offs, the early signs of diabetes (tanda kencing manis), targets if you have diabetes, and when to get tested.
headings: Normal blood sugar levels chart (Malaysia) · What is HbA1c, and what is the normal range? · Prediabetes: the warning stage · Early signs of diabetes (tanda kencing manis) · Blood sugar targets if you have diabetes · Low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) · Who should get tested, and how often · Home glucometer vs lab test · Blood sugar in pregnancy
keywords: Heart & diabetes Normal blood sugar levels Blood glucose HbA1c Diabetes mellitus Kencing manis kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp saringan check-up checkup medical aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Normal fasting blood sugar is below 6.1 mmol/L, and a normal HbA1c is below 5.7%. Malaysia diagnoses diabetes at an HbA1c of 6.3% or more, lower than the 6.5% used by WHO and the American Diabetes Association. Fasting sugar of 7.0 mmol/L or more also means diabetes. Prediabetes is a fasting sugar of 6.1–6.9 mmol/L or an HbA1c of 5.7–6.2%. It usually has no symptoms, and can often be reversed. Warning signs include thirst, passing a lot of urine, waking at night to urinate, tiredness, weight loss and itching or infections around the genitals. Many people have no symptoms at all. Malaysian guidelines advise testing from age 30, yearly, and earlier if you are overweight or have a risk factor. These are the cut-offs in Malaysia’s Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (6th edition), for blood taken from a vein and tested in a laboratory. Test Normal Prediabetes Diabetes Fasting blood sugar (8+ hours without food) Below 6.1 mmol/L 6.1–6.9 mmol/L 7.0 mmol/L or more 2 hours after a glucose drink (OGTT) Below 7.8 mmol/L 7.8–11.0 mmol/L 11.1 mmol/L or more HbA1c Below 5.7% 5.7–6.2% 6.3% or more Random blood sugar (any time) – – 11.1 mmol/L or more mmol/L or mg/dL? Malaysia uses mmol/L. To convert, multiply by 18: for example, 7.0 mmol/L is about 126 mg/dL, and 11.1 mmol/L is about 200 mg/dL. HbA1c is shown as a percentage, or sometimes in mmol/mol (6.3% is 45 mmol/mol). Why Malaysia uses 6.3%, not 6.5% The World Health Organization and the American Diabetes Association diagnose diabetes at an HbA1c of 6.5%. A large Malaysian study found that 6.5% missed too many people with diabetes here, so the Malaysian guideline uses 6.3% , which works across Malay, Chinese and Indian Malaysians. Malaysia also counts a fasting sugar from 6.1 mmol/L as prediabetes, like WHO, while the American Diabetes Association uses 5.6 mmol/L. So an online chart from another country may not match what your doctor tells you. HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin) shows your average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months , by measuring how much sugar has stuck to your red blood cells. You don’t need to fast for it, and one result isn’t thrown off by what you ate yesterday. Below 5.7%: normal. 5.7% to 6.2%: prediabetes. Your doctor may suggest an oral glucose tolerance test to check further. 6.3% or above: diabetes, confirmed with a second test if you have no symptoms. If you have diabetes: the usual target is below 7.0% (see targets below). The test must be done in a laboratory using a standardised method. The quick fingerprick HbA1c machines some clinics use are fine for monitoring diabetes, but Malaysian guidelines say they shouldn’t be used to diagnose it. Prediabetes means your blood sugar is higher than normal but not yet in the diabetes range. It almost never causes symptoms, but without changes many people go on to develop type 2 diabetes. The good news is that it can often be reversed. Losing 5–10% of your body weight if you are overweight, being active for at least 150 minutes a week, and cutting down on sugary drinks, white rice portions and refined snacks all lower your risk. If you have prediabetes, get your blood sugar checked every year . Small, lasting changes to meals and activity can bring prediabetes back to normal. Up to half of people with diabetes have no symptoms . In Malaysia’s National Health and Morbidity Survey 2023, 15.6% of adults (about 3.6 million people) had diabetes, and 5.9% didn’t know it. Among diabetics aged 18 to 29, 84% hadn’t been diagnosed. When symptoms do appear, they include: feeling very thirsty passing a lot of urine, and waking up at night to urinate feeling tired and lethargic feeling hungry more often losing weight without trying itching around the vagina, or soreness and swelling at the tip of the penis, often from repeated yeast infections blurred vision, cuts that heal slowly, and frequent skin or urine infections If you have these signs, see a doctor for a blood test rather than waiting. Read more in our guide to undiagnosed diabetes in young adults . Measure Target for most adults with type 2 diabetes Fasting or before meals 4.4–7.0 mmol/L After meals (at least 90 minutes after eating) 4.4–8.5 mmol/L HbA1c Below 7.0% Your doctor will set a target that suits you. A tighter HbA1c target of 6.5% or below may suit younger, newly diagnosed people at low risk of low sugar. A less strict target of 7.1–8.0% is safer for older people, those with serious heart or kidney disease or dementia, or those who have had severe low sugar episodes. For people on diabetes medicines, especially insulin or certain tablets, blood sugar can drop too low. Hypoglycaemia is a reading below 3.9 mmol/L , and below 3.0 mmol/L is more serious. Signs include shaking, sweating, a fast heartbeat, hunger, confusion and irritability. What to do for low sugar Take 15 g of fast-acting sugar , such as half a glass of fruit juice or regular (not diet) soft drink, or 3 teaspoons of sugar in water. Recheck after 15 minutes, and repeat until your reading is above 3.9 mmol/L, then eat a snack or meal. If someone is drowsy, confused or unconscious, don’t give food or drink by mouth: call 999 . Everyone from age 30 , and every year after that if the result is normal. This is earlier and more often than in some other countries, because diabetes is so common in Malaysia. At any age if your BMI is 23 or more, or your waist is 80 cm or more (women) or 90 cm or more (men), plus any risk factor: a parent, brother or sister with diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, low HDL or high triglycerides, PCOS, an inactive lifestyle, diabetes in a past pregnancy, or a baby born weighing 4 kg or more. Every year if you have prediabetes. Children and teenagers who are overweight and have a risk factor, from puberty or age 10. Free screening is available at Klinik Kesihatan, and through PeKa B40 if you receive STR and are 40 or over. See our guides to free health screening and PeKa B40 . A home glucometer uses a drop of blood from your fingertip. It is very useful for monitoring diabetes day to day, but it is less precise than a laboratory test: good meters can still be about 15% out. Heat and humidity can also affect strips, so store them as instructed. A fingerprick result is a screening result only. If a random fingerprick reading is 7.8 mmol/L or more , or a fasting reading is 5.6 mmol/L or more , Malaysian guidelines say you should have a proper blood test from a vein (fasting sugar, OGTT or HbA1c) to confirm. Is one test enough to diagnose diabetes? If you have symptoms, one high result from a vein blood test can be enough. If you don’t, a second abnormal result is needed, either a repeat test on another day or a glucose and HbA1c from the same sample. Diabetes can also develop during pregnancy (gestational diabetes). In Malaysia, it is diagnosed with a glucose tolerance test if the fasting level is 5.1 mmol/L or more or the 2-hour level is 7.8 mmol/L or more . Women with risk factors are tested at their first antenatal visit, and women aged 25 or over are tested at 24–28 weeks. HbA1c isn’t used to diagnose it. Track your key dates with our pregnancy due date calculator . What is a normal blood sugar level? Under Malaysian guidelines, a normal fasting blood sugar is below 6.1 mmol/L, and below 7.8 mmol/L two hours after a glucose drink. A normal HbA1c is below 5.7%. What is the normal HbA1c range? Below 5.7% is normal. 5.7% to 6.2% is prediabetes, and 6.3% or above is diabetes in Malaysia. For people with diabetes, the usual target is below 7.0%. Why is the HbA1c cut-off for diabetes 6.3% in Malaysia? A Malaysian study found that the 6.5% cut-off used by WHO and the American Diabetes Association missed too many people with diabetes here, so the Malaysian guideline uses 6.3%. What blood sugar level is diabetes? A fasting blood sugar of 7.0 mmol/L or more, a level of 11.1 mmol/L or more two hours after a glucose drink or at any time with symptoms, or an HbA1c of 6.3% or more. Without symptoms, a second test is needed to confirm. What are the early signs of diabetes (tanda kencing manis)? Thirst, passing a lot of urine, waking at night to urinate, tiredness, hunger, unexplained weight loss, and itching or infections around the genitals. Many people have no symptoms, so regular testing matters. What blood sugar level is too low? Below 3.9 mmol/L is low (hypoglycaemia), and below 3.0 mmol/L is more serious. Take 15 g of fast-acting sugar, recheck after 15 minutes, and call 999 if the person is drowsy or unconscious. How to convert mmol/L to mg/dL? Multiply mmol/L by 18. For example, 5.5 mmol/L is about 99 mg/dL and 7.0 mmol/L is about 126 mg/dL. At what age should I check my blood sugar? Malaysian guidelines advise testing from age 30, then yearly. Test earlier if you are overweight and have a risk factor such as a family history of diabetes or high blood pressure.

title: FOMEMA medical check-up: tests, fees, results and appeals explained
desc: Every foreign worker and domestic helper in Peninsular Malaysia must pass a FOMEMA medical examination, now every year. What it tests, how much it costs in 2026, how employers check results, what “unsuitable” means, and how appeals work.
headings: What is FOMEMA? · Who needs a FOMEMA check-up, and when · What the FOMEMA medical examination tests · FOMEMA fees in 2026 · Step by step: from registration to results · How to check FOMEMA results online · Unsuitable results and appeals · Tips for employers and workers
keywords: Guides FOMEMA check-up FOMEMA Foreign worker medical examination kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal klinik doctor doktor gp saringan check-up checkup medical aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: FOMEMA examines blue-collar foreign workers (PLKS permit holders) and foreign domestic helpers. Expatriates and international students use different systems. Since 16 December 2023, every foreign worker must pass the exam every year, before each permit renewal. The exam includes a medical history, physical examination, chest X-ray, blood tests (including HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis and malaria) and urine tests for drugs and pregnancy. From 25 May 2026 the fee is RM226.56 for men and RM237.36 for women, including 8% SST and a RM3 convenience fee. The employer registers and pays. Results go to Immigration within about 7 working days. Employers check them on the FOMEMA portal. Some unsuitable results can be appealed within 2 weeks. FOMEMA is the company appointed by the Government in 1997 to run the compulsory health screening of legal foreign workers, under the supervision of the Ministry of Health. The aim is to make sure workers are fit to work and to stop infectious diseases, such as tuberculosis, from spreading. FOMEMA covers Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan , through about 3,100 panel clinics and 140 laboratories. Foreign worker applications in Sabah and Sarawak are handled under those states’ own arrangements, so check with the state Immigration office there. Its official website is now fomema2u.com.my , and employers use the FOMEMA portal to register workers and see results. Foreign workers on a Temporary Employment Visit Pass (PLKS), in sectors such as manufacturing, construction, plantations, agriculture and services. Foreign domestic helpers. Not expatriates on employment passes, and not international students, who have a separate medical screening through Education Malaysia Global Services (EMGS). When What is needed Before coming to Malaysia A pre-departure medical exam in the worker’s home country After arrival The employer registers the worker with FOMEMA promptly (FOMEMA asks within 72 hours), and the exam must be done within 30 days Every year A FOMEMA exam before each permit renewal. Employers can register up to 3 months before the permit expires Before December 2023, workers were examined yearly for the first 3 years and then every other year. Since 16 December 2023 , the exam is needed every year for all foreign workers. Since 7 September 2026, employers must also confirm the worker’s accommodation address before registration can go ahead. Medical history and physical examination by a FOMEMA panel doctor, including blood pressure. Chest X-ray , mainly to look for tuberculosis (TB). Blood tests for HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis and malaria, and blood group. Hepatitis C and filariasis were added in December 2023. Urine tests for drugs (including opiates and cannabis, with methamphetamine added in December 2023), pregnancy in women, and sugar and protein. Conditions that can make a worker unsuitable include infectious diseases such as TB (including old TB that could become active again), hepatitis B and C, HIV, syphilis, malaria, filariasis and leprosy, as well as cancer, epilepsy, serious psychiatric illness, drug use and pregnancy. Chronic conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes, heart disease, asthma and kidney disease may also lead to an unsuitable result, or to a monitoring programme. According to FOMEMA figures cited by the Malaysian Medical Association, in 2023 the screening detected more than 6,400 cases of TB and more than 3,300 cases of hepatitis B among foreign workers, which is why the checks matter for public health. See our guide to a cough that won’t go away for the signs of TB. Blood tests in the FOMEMA exam include HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis and malaria. Male worker Female worker Examination fee RM207.00 RM217.00 8% SST RM16.56 RM17.36 Convenience fee RM3.00 RM3.00 Total RM226.56 RM237.36 The fees went up from RM190 (male) and RM207 (female) on 16 December 2023, when the new tests were added, and SST was added from 25 May 2026 . If a registration is cancelled, RM29.16 (RM27 plus SST) is kept and the rest refunded. These fees apply in Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan. The employer registers the worker and pays the fee through the FOMEMA portal. Register and pay: the employer, or a registered agency, registers the worker on the FOMEMA portal and pays the fee. Choose a clinic: the employer picks a FOMEMA panel clinic. Find one on the FOMEMA website under “Find Your Nearest Clinic”, or in our directory below. Attend the exam: the worker brings their passport and registration details. The clinic does the examination and takes blood and urine samples. The chest X-ray is done at a FOMEMA-registered X-ray facility, which may be at the same clinic. Certification: the results are reviewed and sent electronically to the Immigration Department, usually within 7 working days . A FOMEMA result is valid for 180 days . Results are checked by the employer : Log in to the FOMEMA portal . Open “Medical Result” . Search by worker code or passport number (up to 10 workers at a time). The result shows Suitable or Unsuitable . For an unsuitable result, the “Reason” column explains why, and the employer can print an unsuitable letter. There is no official public search for workers, so be careful of unofficial websites asking for passport numbers. If a worker is found unsuitable , they can’t continue working in Malaysia. The employer must apply to the Immigration Department for a Check Out Memo and send the worker home. Some results can be appealed. FOMEMA emails the employer if a case is appealable: Register the appeal on the FOMEMA portal within 2 weeks of certification, and submit any extra test results within 4 weeks, or the case is closed. An appeal committee meets weekly. The process takes about 30 days from payment. Some chronic conditions, such as diabetes or high blood pressure, can be cleared under a 6-month monitoring programme . Workers who decline monitoring or miss the final check must be repatriated. Since 20 July 2026 , syphilis can be appealed, with treatment and a 6-month monitoring programme. Not appealable: TB confirmed on chest X-ray, malaria, pregnancy, HIV and hepatitis B. A mismatched blood group needs a new registration rather than an appeal. Register early: up to 3 months before the permit expires, so there is time for an appeal if needed. Make sure the worker’s passport details match the registration exactly. Tell the doctor about any medicines the worker takes, and bring records of known conditions such as diabetes or high blood pressure. Workers with a long cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss should see a doctor before the exam, as TB is treatable. Only use the official FOMEMA website and portal, and never pay anyone who offers to “guarantee” a result. What is FOMEMA? FOMEMA is the company appointed by the Government to run the compulsory medical examination of foreign workers and domestic helpers in Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan, under the supervision of the Ministry of Health. How much is the FOMEMA fee in 2026? From 25 May 2026, RM226.56 for a male worker and RM237.36 for a female worker, including the exam fee (RM207 or RM217), 8% SST and a RM3 convenience fee. How often is the FOMEMA check-up needed? Every year. Since 16 December 2023, all foreign workers must pass a FOMEMA exam before each permit renewal, as well as within 30 days of arriving in Malaysia. What does FOMEMA test for? A medical history, physical examination, chest X-ray, blood tests for HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis, malaria and filariasis, and urine tests for drugs, pregnancy, sugar and protein. How do I check FOMEMA results online? The employer logs in to the FOMEMA portal, opens “Medical Result” and searches by worker code or passport number. Results usually reach Immigration within 7 working days. Can an unsuitable FOMEMA result be appealed? Some can. If FOMEMA says the case is appealable, register the appeal on the portal within 2 weeks of certification. TB confirmed on X-ray, malaria, pregnancy, HIV and hepatitis B can’t be appealed. How long is a FOMEMA result valid? 180 days. Do international students need FOMEMA? No. International students have a separate medical screening through Education Malaysia Global Services (EMGS) at EMGS panel clinics.

title: Psoriasis: symptoms, scalp psoriasis, triggers and treatment in Malaysia
desc: Thick, scaly patches that keep coming back may be psoriasis. How to recognise it (including on the scalp and nails), how it differs from dandruff and kurap, what makes it flare, and the treatments available in Malaysia.
headings: What is psoriasis? · Symptoms: what psoriasis looks like · Scalp psoriasis or dandruff? · Psoriasis, kurap (ringworm) or eczema? · What triggers psoriasis flares? · Psoriatic arthritis: check your joints · Psoriasis, your heart, weight and mood · Psoriasis treatment in Malaysia · When to see a doctor
keywords: Aesthetics & skin Psoriasis Psoriasis Psoriatic arthritis kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october kesihatan mental depression anxiety stress kemurungan mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Psoriasis is an immune-mediated skin disease, not an infection. You can’t catch it or pass it on by touch. Plaque psoriasis, with thick, well-defined, scaly patches, accounts for 80–90% of cases. On brown skin, plaques often look dark brown, purple or grey rather than red. Stress, infections such as strep throat, smoking, alcohol, weight gain, skin injury and some medicines can trigger flares. About 1 in 5 people with psoriasis develop psoriatic arthritis. See a doctor about swollen joints, a “sausage” finger or toe, or morning stiffness. Treatment goes step by step: moisturisers and creams, then light therapy, then tablets or injections. Biologic injections are given in government dermatology clinics. Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory disease that mainly affects the skin and joints. An overactive immune system speeds up the growth of skin cells, which build up into thick, scaly patches called plaques. It runs in families, and usually comes and goes in flares throughout life. It is not contagious . You can’t catch psoriasis from touching someone, sharing a towel or swimming in the same pool. In Malaysia, a study of primary care records in Johor Bahru, quoted in the Ministry of Health’s 2024 psoriasis guideline, found that about 3 in every 1,000 people (0.34%) have psoriasis, with higher rates among Indians (0.54%) than Malays (0.38%) and Chinese (0.29%). The Malaysian Psoriasis Registry, which follows more than 8,800 patients, shows symptoms typically start in the 30s , with a second peak in the 60s. Children can get it too. About 1 in 4 patients has a family member with psoriasis. Thick, raised, scaly plaques with sharp edges, often on both sides of the body, on the scalp, elbows, knees, lower back and buttock crease. Colour depends on skin tone. On lighter skin, plaques look pink or red with silvery-white scale. On brown skin, they often look dark brown, purple or greyish , and can leave dark or light marks for 3 to 12 months after they clear. Itch: more than 3 in 4 Malaysian patients in the registry report itching. Nail changes: small pits on the nails, or nails lifting away from the nail bed. More than half of Malaysian adults with psoriasis have nail involvement. Types of psoriasis: Type What it looks like Plaque (the most common, 80–90%) Thick, scaly, well-defined patches on the scalp, elbows, knees and back Guttate Many small, drop-shaped spots, often appearing suddenly in children and young adults after a strep throat infection Inverse (flexural) Smooth, shiny patches without much scale in skin folds: armpits, groin, under the breasts Pustular Pus-filled spots that aren’t infected, on the palms and soles or, rarely, all over the body Erythrodermic Rare: red, inflamed skin over most of the body. This is an emergency About 1 in 3 Malaysian adults with psoriasis have it on the scalp, face or genitals. Scalp psoriasis is often mistaken for dandruff (seborrhoeic dermatitis), and the two can occur together. Scalp psoriasis Dandruff / seborrhoeic dermatitis Scale Thick, dry, silvery, stuck on Greasy, yellowish, flakes off easily Edges Sharp, raised plaques Less defined Spread Often goes past the hairline onto the forehead, neck or behind the ears Usually stays within the scalp, eyebrows and sides of the nose Elsewhere Often plaques on elbows, knees or nails too Usually no plaques elsewhere Medicated scalp gels, coal tar shampoos and combination steroid and vitamin D gels prescribed by a doctor work better than ordinary anti-dandruff shampoo for scalp psoriasis. Don’t pick or scratch off the scale, as injuring the skin can make psoriasis worse. Kurap (ringworm, tinea) is a fungal infection. It usually forms an itchy ring with a clearer centre and a scaly, spreading edge, and is often on one side of the body. A doctor can confirm it by looking at a skin scraping under a microscope. Eczema tends to have less sharply defined edges, often appears in the inner elbows and behind the knees, and is usually itchier. Psoriasis plaques are thicker and more often on the outer elbows and knees. See our guide to itchy skin, eczema and hives . Be careful with steroid creams and “miracle” creams Steroid creams used on a fungal infection can hide it and help it spread, so get a diagnosis before treating a rash for weeks. Avoid unregistered creams sold online or at markets: the Ministry of Health has found steroids such as betamethasone hidden in some cosmetics, which can thin and damage the skin. Check that a product is registered on the NPRA website or the NPRA Product Status app. Stress: the most common trigger reported by Malaysian patients (about 2 in 3). Infections: especially strep throat, which can set off guttate psoriasis. See our guide to coughs and chest infections . Skin injury: cuts, scratches, insect bites or sunburn can cause new plaques at the injured spot (the Koebner phenomenon). Smoking, alcohol and weight gain. Some medicines: including certain blood pressure tablets (beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors), lithium, antimalarials, some anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs), and stopping oral steroids suddenly. Never stop a prescribed medicine on your own; ask your doctor whether it could be a trigger. Some sunlight often helps psoriasis, but about 3 in 10 Malaysian patients say too much sun makes it worse. Avoid sunburn. About 1 in 5 people with psoriasis develop psoriatic arthritis (19% in the Malaysian registry), and many cases go undiagnosed. In most Malaysian patients, the skin problem comes first and the joints later. Untreated, it can permanently damage joints, so the Ministry of Health guideline recommends checking for it at least once a year. See a doctor if you have: painful, swollen joints, especially in the fingers and toes a whole finger or toe swollen like a sausage (dactylitis) pain where tendons attach to bone, such as the back of the heel back pain and stiffness that is worse in the morning and better with movement, or morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes Psoriasis isn’t only skin deep. The inflammation affects the whole body, and people with psoriasis, especially moderate to severe psoriasis, have a higher risk of heart attack and stroke. Among Malaysian adults in the psoriasis registry: 63% were overweight or obese 29% had high blood pressure 23% had high cholesterol 19% had diabetes It is worth having your blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar checked regularly. See our guides to blood pressure and cholesterol and normal blood sugar levels . Psoriasis is also linked to depression and anxiety, and more than 1 in 3 Malaysian patients say it has a very large effect on their quality of life. If it is getting you down, tell your doctor. See our guide to anxiety . The Ministry of Health’s guideline, Management of Psoriasis (2nd edition, 2024), sets out treatment step by step. The aim is clear or almost clear skin (less than 3% of the body affected) and little effect on daily life within 12 to 16 weeks. Moisturisers every day , to soften scale and reduce itch. Creams and ointments for mild psoriasis: steroid creams are first-line. Doctors may add a vitamin D cream (calcipotriol, alone or combined with a steroid), coal tar, salicylic acid to lift scale, or dithranol for stubborn plaques. Gentler non-steroid creams are used on the face and skin folds. Light therapy (narrowband UVB phototherapy) for more widespread psoriasis, given 2 to 3 times a week at hospital dermatology units. It is not available at every centre. Tablets such as methotrexate (the most commonly used), acitretin or ciclosporin, for moderate to severe psoriasis. They need regular blood tests. Acitretin must not be taken by women who may become pregnant without reliable contraception. Biologic injections and newer oral treatments , which target specific parts of the immune system, for severe psoriasis or when other treatments haven’t worked. Biologics are given in government dermatology clinics. Cost is a barrier, and funding can come from sources such as the civil service scheme for government staff, hospital funds or medical aid funds. Psoriasis is considered moderate to severe if it covers more than 10% of your body (your palm and fingers are about 1%), affects the face, scalp, palms, soles or genitals, or seriously affects your daily life. In those cases, you may need light therapy, tablets or injections rather than creams alone. Most mild psoriasis can be managed by a GP. Widespread or stubborn psoriasis is referred to a hospital dermatology clinic. You have a scaly rash that hasn’t gone away, and you aren’t sure what it is. Your psoriasis isn’t improving after 12 weeks of creams, or covers a large area. It affects your face, scalp, hands, feet or genitals, or is affecting your sleep, work or mood. You have joint pain, swelling or morning stiffness. A GP or Klinik Kesihatan can diagnose and treat most mild psoriasis, check for related conditions, and refer you to a government hospital dermatology clinic if you need specialist care. Get urgent medical help Go to a hospital emergency department if your skin suddenly becomes red and inflamed over most of your body, or you develop widespread pus-filled spots with fever, chills or feeling very unwell. These rare forms of psoriasis can be dangerous. Is psoriasis contagious? No. Psoriasis is caused by the immune system, not an infection. You can’t catch it or pass it to others by touch, sharing towels or swimming. Can psoriasis be cured? There is no cure yet, but treatment can clear or nearly clear the skin for most people. Psoriasis tends to come and go, so many people need ongoing or repeated treatment. How do I know if it is scalp psoriasis or dandruff? Scalp psoriasis has thick, dry, silvery scale with sharp edges that often spreads past the hairline, and there are often plaques elsewhere on the body. Dandruff has greasy, yellowish flakes that come off easily. Is it psoriasis or kurap (ringworm)? Kurap is a fungal infection that usually forms an itchy ring with a clearer centre and a spreading edge. Psoriasis plaques are thick and scaly throughout, often on both elbows or knees. A doctor can check a skin scraping to be sure. What triggers psoriasis? Common triggers include stress, infections such as strep throat, skin injury, smoking, alcohol, weight gain and some medicines, including certain blood pressure tablets and lithium. What is psoriatic arthritis? It is joint inflammation linked to psoriasis, affecting about 1 in 5 people with psoriasis. Signs include swollen, painful joints, a swollen “sausage” finger or toe, heel pain and morning stiffness. See a doctor early to prevent joint damage. Are biologic injections available in Malaysia? Yes. Several biologics and newer oral treatments are used in Malaysia, including in government dermatology clinics, for severe psoriasis or when other treatments haven’t worked.

title: Anxiety: the signs, how to cope, and when to get help (including exam stress)
desc: Everyone worries, but anxiety that won’t switch off can take over sleep, work and studies. The signs, self-help that works, what the evidence says about magnesium, where to get help in Malaysia, and how to handle exam stress.
headings: What is anxiety? (Apakah anxiety?) · Common types of anxiety · Signs and symptoms of anxiety · How to overcome anxiety: self-help that works · Does magnesium help anxiety and sleep? · Treatment for anxiety · Where to get help in Malaysia · Exam stress and SPM
keywords: Mental wellbeing Anxiety Anxiety disorder Gangguan kebimbangan kesihatan mental depression anxiety stress kemurungan kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Anxiety becomes a disorder when worry is intense, hard to control, lasts for months and affects daily life. About 1 in 17 people worldwide has an anxiety disorder. Physical symptoms are common: a racing heart, breathlessness, stomach upset, tense muscles and poor sleep. Regular exercise, sleep, slow breathing, less caffeine and alcohol, and techniques such as “worry time” help many people. Talking therapy, especially cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), is the first-line treatment. Medicines can help when therapy isn’t enough. Help is available through Klinik Kesihatan, MyMinda in MySejahtera, and Talian HEAL 15555. If you are thinking of harming yourself, call 999 or Befrienders on 03-7627 2929. Anxiety is the body’s natural response to threat or pressure: a feeling of worry, unease or fear. In small doses it is useful, helping you prepare for an exam or stay alert in danger. It becomes an anxiety disorder when the fear and worry are intense, out of proportion, hard to control, and last for months, causing distress or getting in the way of daily life. The World Health Organization estimates that 470 million people , about 1 in 17 worldwide, live with an anxiety disorder, yet fewer than 3 in 10 who need treatment receive any. In Malaysia, the National Health and Morbidity Survey 2017 found symptoms of anxiety in about 2 in 5 teenagers aged 13 to 17. In October 2026, the Health Minister said young people aged 16 to 19 have the highest rate of depression, at 7.9%. Calls to the Ministry’s Talian HEAL helpline more than doubled from 42,990 in 2024 to 90,981 in 2025. Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD): worrying about many different things, most days, for 6 months or more, and finding it hard to stop. Panic disorder: repeated, sudden panic attacks, with a racing heart, chest pain, breathlessness, sweating, trembling, nausea, or a fear of dying or losing control. Attacks usually last 5 to 20 minutes. They are frightening but not dangerous. Health anxiety: constant worry about being ill, checking your body, searching symptoms online and seeking reassurance. Social anxiety: intense fear of being judged or embarrassed in social situations. What about BPD? Borderline personality disorder is often searched alongside anxiety, but it is a different condition. It affects how a person manages emotions and relationships, with intense mood swings, impulsive behaviour and unstable relationships. It can occur together with anxiety, and specialised talking therapies help many people improve. In your mind In your body Constant worry, fearing the worst Racing or pounding heart Feeling restless or on edge Breathlessness, tight chest Irritability Stomach upset, nausea, needing the toilet Difficulty concentrating, mind going blank Tense muscles, headaches Avoiding places or situations Poor sleep, tiredness, dizziness Panic attack or heart attack? If you have chest pain that feels tight or squeezing, spreads to your arm, neck or jaw, or comes with severe breathlessness, sweating or grey skin, treat it as an emergency and call 999 , even if you have had panic attacks before. Doctors would much rather check and find it is anxiety. See our guide to heart attack warning signs . Breathe slowly. Breathe in gently through your nose for a count of 5, then out through your mouth for a count of 5. Practise for 5 minutes a day, not just when anxious. Move every day. Regular exercise, even a brisk walk, is one of the most effective ways to reduce anxiety. Protect your sleep. Keep regular sleep and wake times, and wind down without screens before bed. Cut down caffeine and alcohol. Coffee, energy drinks and alcohol can all make anxiety worse. Set a “worry time”. Write worries down when they come, and save them for a set 15-minute slot each day. Many lose their power by then. Challenge anxious thoughts. Ask yourself what you would tell a friend who had the same thought. Face fears gradually. Avoiding situations keeps anxiety going. Take small, manageable steps towards them. Ground yourself. When anxiety rises, name 5 things you can see, 4 you can feel, 3 you can hear, 2 you can smell and 1 you can taste. You can do a confidential self-assessment and find self-care resources in MyMinda , the mental health section of the MySejahtera app. Small daily habits, such as exercise, sleep and slow breathing, make a real difference to anxiety. Magnesium supplements are popular for anxiety and sleep, but the evidence is weak . A 2017 review of 18 studies found a possible benefit only in people already prone to anxiety, and rated the quality of the studies as poor. A 2021 analysis in older adults with insomnia found people fell asleep about 17 minutes sooner, but the evidence was low quality. Magnesium isn’t a substitute for treatment. High doses can cause diarrhoea, and it can interact with some medicines and build up in people with kidney disease. Ask a doctor or pharmacist before taking it. Talking therapy: cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is the first-line treatment for most anxiety disorders. It helps you understand and change the thoughts and habits that keep anxiety going, usually over a set number of sessions. Medicine: if therapy alone isn’t enough, doctors may prescribe a daily antidepressant from the SSRI or SNRI group, which also treat anxiety. They take a few weeks to work and shouldn’t be stopped suddenly. Sedatives such as benzodiazepines are generally only used briefly in a crisis, because they can cause dependence. Most people with anxiety improve with treatment. The sooner you get help, the easier it usually is. A GP or Klinik Kesihatan: a good first step. Government health clinics charge Malaysians a small fee and can screen for anxiety and depression, start treatment and refer you to a psychiatrist or psychologist. MENTARI community mental health centres: run by the Ministry of Health in many districts. Private psychologists, counsellors and psychiatrists: available in most cities, usually by appointment. Talian HEAL 15555: the Ministry of Health’s free psychosocial support line, staffed by counsellors, 8am to midnight every day. If you are in crisis If you are thinking of harming yourself or ending your life, call 999 or go to the nearest emergency department. You can also call Befrienders KL on 03-7627 2929 , free and confidential, 24 hours a day, or Talian Kasih on 15999 . More helplines are listed in our mental health helplines guide . More than 420,000 students sit the SPM written papers from 23 November to 17 December 2026 . Some stress can help concentration, but too much gets in the way. For students: Make a realistic revision timetable, with regular short breaks. Sleep 8 to 10 hours, and avoid all-night cramming. Sleep helps your memory. Keep moving: a short walk or exercise between study sessions clears the mind. Go easy on energy drinks and coffee. Talk to someone: a parent, teacher, school counsellor or friend. For parents: watch for signs such as worry, headaches or stomach aches, poor sleep, irritability, changes in appetite, low mood or hopelessness. Keep expectations realistic, avoid adding pressure, and make sure your child eats and sleeps well. If anxiety or low mood is severe, lasts after the exams, or your child talks about self-harm, see a doctor promptly. What is anxiety? (Apakah anxiety?) Anxiety is a feeling of worry, unease or fear. It becomes an anxiety disorder when the worry is intense, hard to control, lasts for months and affects daily life. It is common and treatable. How can I overcome anxiety? Regular exercise, good sleep, slow breathing, cutting down caffeine and alcohol, setting a daily “worry time” and gradually facing feared situations all help. If anxiety is affecting your life, see a doctor about talking therapy such as CBT. Does magnesium help with anxiety and sleep? The evidence is weak. Small, low-quality studies suggest a possible small benefit for some people. It isn’t a substitute for treatment, so ask a doctor or pharmacist before taking supplements. How do I know if it is a panic attack or a heart attack? Panic attacks usually peak within minutes and pass within about 20 minutes. But chest pain that feels tight or squeezing, spreads to the arm, neck or jaw, or comes with severe breathlessness should be treated as an emergency. Call 999. Is BPD the same as anxiety? No. Borderline personality disorder affects how a person manages emotions and relationships. It can occur alongside anxiety, but it is a separate condition with its own treatments. Where can I get free mental health support in Malaysia? Talian HEAL 15555 (8am to midnight daily), Befrienders KL 03-7627 2929 (24 hours), Talian Kasih 15999, and MyMinda in MySejahtera. Government health clinics offer low-cost assessment and referral.

title: HIV in Malaysia: symptoms, testing, PrEP and treatment
desc: Around 3,000 Malaysians are diagnosed with HIV every year, most of them young men. Early symptoms, the difference between HIV and AIDS, where to get tested (including self-tests), free PrEP, and why treatment means a long, healthy life.
headings: HIV in Malaysia today · HIV vs AIDS: what is the difference? · Early HIV symptoms, including the HIV rash · Where and how to get tested in Malaysia · Preventing HIV: PrEP and PEP · Treatment for HIV · The premarital HIV test · Living with HIV, without stigma
keywords: Prevention HIV in Malaysia HIV/AIDS HIV/AIDS mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal klinik doctor doktor gp saringan check-up checkup medical
body: Malaysia records around 3,000 to 3,300 new HIV cases a year. In 2024 there were 3,185. 90% were men, most aged 20 to 39, and almost all infections were sexually transmitted. Early HIV can cause a flu-like illness and rash 2 to 6 weeks after infection, but many people have no symptoms. The only way to know is to get tested. HIV testing is available at government health clinics, NGO community centres and private clinics. Self-test kits are sold at selected pharmacies and online. PrEP, a daily pill that prevents HIV, is free at selected government health clinics. PEP must be started within 72 hours after a possible exposure. With treatment, people with HIV live long, healthy lives. When the virus is undetectable, it isn’t passed on through sex (U=U). Malaysia has recorded an average of about 3,170 new HIV cases a year since 2018, according to the Ministry of Health. There were 3,185 in 2024, and a preliminary 3,004 in 2025. That is less than half the peak of nearly 7,000 a year in the early 2000s. 90% of new cases are men , and three-quarters are aged 20 to 39. In 2023, 44% were in their twenties. 96% of new infections are sexually transmitted , around two-thirds among men who have sex with men. Infections from sharing needles, once the main route, are now rare. In 2024, 135 new cases were adolescents aged 10 to 19, and 222 were students in higher education. An estimated 85,000 people live with HIV in Malaysia. About 16% don’t know they have it. Malaysia was the first country in the Western Pacific to be validated by the WHO for eliminating mother-to-child transmission of HIV, in 2018, and kept that status in October 2026. About 99% of pregnant women with HIV now receive treatment. HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) is the virus. It attacks CD4 cells, part of the immune system. AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) is the most advanced stage of untreated HIV. It is diagnosed when the CD4 count falls below 200, or when certain serious infections or cancers develop. The WHO now calls this “advanced HIV disease”. Without treatment, HIV usually takes years to progress to AIDS. With treatment, most people never develop AIDS. U=U: undetectable = untransmittable. People with HIV who take their treatment and keep the virus at undetectable levels do not pass HIV on to their sexual partners. This is backed by the WHO and the US CDC. Some people get a short, flu-like illness 2 to 6 weeks after infection, as the body reacts to the virus: Fever, sore throat, tiredness and aching muscles Swollen glands in the neck, armpits or groin A rash : usually flat and slightly raised red spots spread across the body, lasting a short time Occasionally mouth or genital ulcers These symptoms usually go away within a few weeks. After that, HIV often causes no symptoms for many years , while it slowly damages the immune system. Early HIV symptoms are the same for men and women, and they look like many other common infections. You can’t tell from symptoms alone. The only way to know your HIV status is to get tested. Government health clinics (Klinik Kesihatan): HIV screening has been offered free for Malaysians, apart from the registration fee. Results are confidential. Community and NGO testing: the Malaysian AIDS Council and partner organisations offer friendly, confidential testing and counselling. Private clinics and hospitals: for a fee, usually with fast results. Self-test kits: since November 2024, HIV self-test kits have been sold at selected pharmacies and online through the TestNow programme, run with the Ministry of Health and the Malaysian AIDS Foundation. A positive self-test must be confirmed at a clinic. The window period: a test can miss a very recent infection. According to the US CDC, a laboratory blood test can detect HIV from 18 to 45 days after exposure, and rapid finger-prick and self-tests from 23 to 90 days . If you test early, test again after the window period. A laboratory blood test can detect HIV earlier than rapid and self-tests. PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) is medicine taken by HIV-negative people to prevent infection. Taken as prescribed, it is highly effective. Since 2023, PrEP has been offered free at selected government health clinics. By mid-2025, 35 clinics offered it and more than 9,300 people had started it. It is also available at private clinics. PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis) is a 28-day course of HIV medicine taken after a possible exposure, such as condomless sex or sexual assault. It must be started within 72 hours , and the sooner the better. It is available at selected government hospitals, university hospitals and private clinics. The Malaysian AIDS Council lists providers on its website. Go straight away rather than waiting. Condoms also protect against HIV and other sexually transmitted infections. HIV is treated with antiretroviral therapy (ART) : a combination of medicines taken every day. ART doesn’t cure HIV, but it stops the virus multiplying, lets the immune system recover, and prevents transmission. Treatment is started as soon as possible after diagnosis. First-line HIV treatment has been provided free to Malaysian citizens at Ministry of Health facilities since 2006. Around 50,700 people were on treatment in 2024. Taking medicine every day and keeping regular check-ups is the key to staying well. HIV screening is compulsory for all Muslim couples before marriage in Malaysia. It started in Johor in 2001 and has been nationwide since 2009. The test is done at government health clinics . You can book an appointment through MySejahtera. If you apply through the state Islamic religious department, you’ll get a screening form (borang) for your couple. Bring it to the test. The result is valid for 6 months . If the result is positive, you’ll be offered counselling at the health clinic and the religious office. For non-Muslim couples, premarital HIV screening is voluntary, but it is a good idea for both partners. HIV can affect anyone, and stigma stops people from getting tested and treated. People with HIV can work, marry, have children who are HIV-negative, and live full lives. If you face discrimination in a health setting, the Malaysian AIDS Council (MAC) can help, through its MAC CARE service. Complaints about government facilities can also be made through the government’s public complaints system. What is the difference between HIV and AIDS? HIV is the virus. AIDS is the most advanced stage of untreated HIV, when the immune system is badly damaged. With treatment, most people with HIV never develop AIDS. What does an HIV rash look like? It is usually a short-lived rash of flat or slightly raised red spots spread across the body, appearing 2 to 6 weeks after infection, often with fever and sore throat. Many other infections look the same, so only a test can tell. What are the symptoms of HIV in men? (Simptom HIV lelaki) Early symptoms are the same for men and women: fever, sore throat, swollen glands, rash, tiredness and aching muscles, 2 to 6 weeks after infection. Many people have no symptoms. The only way to know is to test. Is HIV testing free in Malaysia? HIV screening at government health clinics has been free for Malaysians, apart from the registration fee. Community testing through NGOs is also available. Private clinics charge a fee. How do I do the premarital HIV test? (Borang HIV pra perkahwinan) Muslim couples must be screened at a government health clinic before marriage. Book through MySejahtera, and bring the screening form from your state Islamic religious department. Results are valid for 6 months. Where can I get PrEP in Malaysia? PrEP is free at selected government health clinics, and also available at private clinics. The Malaysian AIDS Council lists providers on its website.

title: Stomach pain and “gastric”: what the location can mean, and when it’s an emergency
desc: Most stomach aches are harmless, but some need urgent care. What pain in different parts of the tummy can mean, what Malaysians call “gastric”, H. pylori, which medicines help, and the warning signs in adults and children.
headings: What is “gastric”? (Apa itu gastrik?) · Causes of gastric pain · What the location of the pain can mean · How to ease gastric and indigestion · Food and lifestyle for gastric · Children with stomach pain and vomiting · When stomach pain is an emergency
keywords: Guides Stomach pain and gastric Abdominal pain Sakit perut denggi aedes nyamuk mosquito kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital
body: What Malaysians call “gastric” is usually indigestion (dyspepsia) or gastritis: burning or gnawing pain in the upper middle tummy, bloating, early fullness and nausea. A common cause is the H. pylori bacteria, which is far more common among Malaysians of Indian and Chinese descent than Malays. It can be tested for with a breath test and treated with antibiotics. Pain that starts around the belly button and moves to the lower right may be appendicitis. One-sided lower pain in a woman who could be pregnant needs urgent assessment. Antacids and alginates help occasional indigestion. Don’t take pharmacy omeprazole for more than 2 weeks without seeing a doctor. Call 999 for sudden severe pain, vomiting blood, black stools, or pain with chest pain or breathlessness. In Malaysia, “gastric” (gastrik) is used for several stomach problems that cause similar symptoms: Indigestion (dyspepsia): pain or burning in the upper middle tummy, bloating, feeling full quickly, burping and nausea. In most people tests find no damage, which doctors call functional dyspepsia . Gastritis: inflammation of the stomach lining, often caused by H. pylori bacteria, painkillers such as ibuprofen and aspirin, or alcohol. Stomach (peptic) ulcer: a sore in the lining of the stomach or duodenum, causing burning pain that is often worse at night. Acid reflux (GORD): heartburn, a burning feeling rising from the stomach into the chest, and a sour taste. Indigestion is common in Malaysia: a study in Kuala Lumpur found it in about 1 in 4 adults. H. pylori: a bacteria that infects the stomach lining and is the most common cause of chronic gastritis and ulcers. In Malaysian studies it is much more common among people of Indian and Chinese descent than Malays. In one Kelantan study, it was found in 29% of Indian, 24% of Chinese and 7% of Malay patients. Painkillers: regular use of anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen, diclofenac and aspirin. Smoking and alcohol. Triggers: large, fatty or spicy meals, coffee, chocolate, being overweight, pregnancy and stress can bring on symptoms. The NHS notes that spicy food and stress don’t cause ulcers, but can make symptoms worse. Skipping meals is often blamed for gastric. Studies have found links between irregular meals and indigestion, but haven’t shown that it is a cause. The location of pain gives clues, but it isn’t a diagnosis. Many conditions can cause pain in more than one place. Where it hurts Possible causes Upper middle (atas tengah) Indigestion, gastritis, ulcer, acid reflux. Less often, pancreatitis (severe pain spreading to the back) or a heart attack Upper right Gallstones (severe pain under the right ribs, lasting up to several hours), liver problems Upper left Gastritis, ulcer, pancreas or spleen problems Around the belly button, moving to the lower right Appendicitis Lower left (sebelah kiri) Constipation, trapped wind, diverticulitis (more common in older adults), kidney stones Side or back, spreading to the groin Kidney stones, kidney infection Lower tummy, all over Stomach bug, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), urine infection In women , lower tummy pain on one side can also be caused by period pain, ovulation pain, an ovarian cyst, endometriosis, pelvic infection, or an ectopic pregnancy . If there is any chance you could be pregnant, one-sided pain, especially with bleeding, dizziness or shoulder-tip pain, needs urgent assessment. See our pregnancy guide . Is it gastric or your heart? A heart attack can feel like indigestion: a burning or heavy feeling in the upper tummy or chest, with sweating, nausea, breathlessness, or pain spreading to the arm, neck or jaw. If you have these symptoms, especially with diabetes, high blood pressure or if you smoke, call 999. See our heart attack guide . Pharmacy medicines (ubat gastrik di farmasi): Antacids and alginates neutralise acid or form a protective layer. They work quickly for occasional symptoms. Take them with or after food, and don’t rely on them long term. Acid-reducing medicines such as omeprazole (a proton pump inhibitor) or famotidine reduce stomach acid. Don’t take omeprazole bought from a pharmacy for more than 2 weeks without seeing a doctor. Long-term use needs medical supervision, and it can hide the symptoms of more serious conditions. Avoid ibuprofen, diclofenac and aspirin unless a doctor has prescribed them. Use paracetamol for pain instead. H. pylori: test and treat. If you have ongoing indigestion, your doctor may test for H. pylori, usually with a urea breath test . You need to stop acid-reducing medicines and antibiotics for 2 to 4 weeks beforehand, so ask your doctor. If the test is positive, the Malaysian H. pylori consensus recommends a 14-day course of an acid-reducing medicine plus antibiotics, followed by a repeat breath test to confirm the infection has gone. Don’t take pharmacy acid-reducing medicines for more than 2 weeks without seeing a doctor. There is no single “gastric diet”. Studies haven’t shown that cutting out particular foods works for everyone. What helps most people: Eat smaller meals , and avoid eating 3 to 4 hours before bed. Notice and avoid your own trigger foods , such as spicy, fatty or fried food, coffee or chocolate. Cut down on alcohol, and stop smoking. Lose weight if you are overweight. Raise the head of your bed slightly if you get heartburn at night. In children, stomach pain with vomiting is usually a stomach bug (gastroenteritis). Vomiting usually stops within 1 to 2 days and diarrhoea within 5 to 7 days. The main risk is dehydration : Give small, frequent sips of water or oral rehydration salts (ORS). Avoid fruit juice and fizzy drinks. Watch for fewer wet nappies, dark urine, a dry mouth, or a child who is unusually sleepy. In Malaysia, remember dengue : severe tummy pain and persistent vomiting are dengue warning signs, often appearing as the fever comes down. See our dengue guide . Get urgent care for a child with Green, yellow-green or bloody vomit Pain that moves to the lower right, or gets steadily worse over a few hours, especially with fever Blood in the stool Drowsiness, not responding normally, or a stiff neck Signs of dehydration, or vomiting for more than 2 days Call 999 or go to an emergency department for Sudden, severe stomach pain, or pain that suddenly gets much worse Vomiting blood, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds Black, sticky stools, or heavy bleeding from the bottom A hard, swollen tummy that is very painful to touch Being unable to pass urine, stool or wind, with vomiting Stomach pain with chest pain or difficulty breathing Stomach pain during pregnancy See a doctor soon if you have indigestion with unexplained weight loss, difficulty swallowing, persistent vomiting, anaemia, or a family history of stomach cancer, or if new indigestion starts in middle age. Your doctor may arrange an endoscopy, a camera test to look inside the stomach. What is gastric? (Apa itu gastrik?) In Malaysia, “gastric” usually means indigestion or gastritis: burning or gnawing pain in the upper middle tummy, bloating, feeling full quickly and nausea. Common causes include H. pylori bacteria, painkillers such as ibuprofen, smoking and alcohol. Why does the left side of my stomach hurt? (Kenapa perut sakit sebelah kiri?) Common causes include trapped wind, constipation and gastritis. In older adults, diverticulitis can cause lower left pain, and kidney stones cause pain in the side. In women, ovarian cysts or period pain are possible. See a doctor if the pain is severe, persistent, or comes with fever or vomiting. What is the best gastric medicine at a pharmacy? Antacids and alginates give quick relief for occasional symptoms. Acid-reducing medicines such as omeprazole help more persistent symptoms, but shouldn’t be taken for more than 2 weeks without seeing a doctor. What should I eat if I have gastric? There is no single gastric diet. Eat smaller meals, avoid eating late at night, and avoid foods that trigger your own symptoms, such as spicy, fatty or fried food, coffee or alcohol. My child has stomach pain and is vomiting. What should I do? Most cases are a stomach bug. Give small sips of oral rehydration salts and watch for dehydration. Get urgent care for green or bloody vomit, pain moving to the lower right, severe or worsening pain, or a drowsy child. Can gastric pain be a heart attack? Yes, sometimes. A heart attack can feel like indigestion, with burning in the upper tummy or chest. Call 999 if it comes with sweating, breathlessness, or pain spreading to the arm, neck or jaw.

title: Headaches: common types, why they keep coming back, and warning signs
desc: Most headaches are tension headaches or migraine, and are not dangerous. How to tell the types apart, why frequent painkillers can make headaches worse, whether koyok and balms work, and the warning signs that need urgent care.
headings: Common types of headache · Pain at the back of the head and neck · Why do I keep getting headaches? (Punca kerap sakit kepala) · How to get rid of a headache · When a headache is an emergency · Headaches in children
keywords: Guides Headaches Headache Sakit kepala darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Tension headaches feel like a tight band around the head, on both sides. Migraine is usually a throbbing pain, often one-sided, with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound. Taking painkillers on more than 2 or 3 days a week can cause medication-overuse headache, a common reason headaches keep coming back. Stress, poor sleep, skipped meals, dehydration, posture, screen time and alcohol are common triggers. A headache diary helps find yours. Menthol or peppermint balms have some evidence for tension headaches. Cluster headaches need specific treatment from a doctor. Call 999 for a sudden, extremely severe headache, or a headache with weakness, confusion, slurred speech, a stiff neck and fever, or after a head injury. Type What it feels like How long Tension-type headache Pressing or tight, like a band around the head, on both sides. Mild to moderate. Often with tight neck and shoulder muscles. 30 minutes to several days Migraine Throbbing, often on one side, moderate to severe, worse with activity. Nausea or vomiting, and sensitivity to light and sound. Some people get an aura first, such as flashing lights. 4 hours to 3 days Cluster headache Very severe, one-sided pain around or above the eye, with a red, watery eye, runny nose or drooping eyelid on the same side. Restlessness. Comes in “clusters” lasting weeks or months. 15 minutes to 3 hours, up to several times a day Medication-overuse headache A daily or near-daily headache in someone taking painkillers frequently Persistent A community study in Malaysia found that about 1 in 4 adults had tension-type headaches and about 1 in 11 had migraine in a year, more often women. “Sinus headache” is often migraine. In one study, most people who believed they had sinus headaches actually met the criteria for migraine. A true sinus infection usually comes with a blocked nose, thick discharge and fever. Headaches at the back of the head, near the neck, are usually caused by: Tension-type headache , often with tight neck and shoulder muscles from stress or long hours at a desk or phone. Neck problems (cervicogenic headache): pain that starts in the neck, often with stiffness and pain when moving the neck. Occipital neuralgia: brief, sharp, shooting or electric pains from the base of the skull, with a tender scalp. A low, firm pillow, regular breaks from screens, stretching, and a warm or cold pack on the neck can help. See a doctor for back-of-head pain after a fall or injury, or with any of the warning signs below. A headache diary helps your doctor work out the type of headache and its triggers. Common triggers, according to the NHS: Stress, anxiety and poor or irregular sleep Skipping meals, and not drinking enough water Poor posture, and long hours looking at screens Eyesight problems. Get your eyes tested if headaches come with reading or screen use Alcohol, and too much (or suddenly cutting down) caffeine Hormonal changes, such as periods and menopause Colds, flu and sinus infections In the Malaysian study, more than half of people with migraine or tension headaches said sun exposure brought them on. Too many painkillers can cause headaches Taking simple painkillers on 15 or more days a month, or combination painkillers or triptans on 10 or more days a month, can cause medication-overuse headache , the most common cause of daily headaches. Try to keep painkillers to no more than 2 or 3 days a week. If you are already taking them most days, see a doctor. Stopping, with support, usually brings improvement. Keep a headache diary. Note when headaches happen, how bad they are, what you were doing, what you ate, how you slept, and what medicine you took. Patterns often appear within a few weeks. Simple painkillers: paracetamol, ibuprofen or aspirin work for most tension headaches. Take them early in a migraine attack. Don’t give aspirin to anyone under 16. In pregnancy, paracetamol is the usual first choice. Rest, water and food: drink water, eat if you’ve skipped a meal, and rest in a quiet, dark room during a migraine. Relax your neck and shoulders: gentle stretches, a warm shower or a warm pack. Koyok, menthol and peppermint balms: small studies have found that 10% peppermint oil or menthol applied to the forehead and temples eased tension headaches and migraine better than a placebo. Many patches also contain methyl salicylate, which is similar to aspirin, so avoid them if you are allergic to aspirin, take blood thinners, or on broken skin, and check the label before using them on children. For migraine , a doctor may prescribe a triptan , a specific migraine medicine, and anti-sickness medicine. If you have frequent migraines, daily preventive medicines can reduce how often they happen. Newer injectable preventive treatments exist, and a neurologist can advise whether they suit you. Cluster headaches don’t respond to ordinary painkillers. They are treated with high-flow oxygen or a triptan injection or nasal spray, so see a doctor for a diagnosis and a treatment plan. Call 999 or go to an emergency department for a headache That comes on suddenly and is extremely painful , reaching its worst within a minute (a “thunderclap” headache) With weakness or numbness of the face, arm or leg, slurred speech, confusion, or difficulty walking or balancing. These can be signs of a stroke. With a high temperature, stiff neck, sensitivity to light, or a rash that doesn’t fade when pressed with a glass After a head injury in the last 3 months With a seizure, drowsiness, or loss of vision See a doctor urgently for a headache that: is new, especially if you are over 50, or different from your usual headaches is getting steadily worse, wakes you from sleep, or comes with vomiting gets worse when you cough, sneeze or bend over comes with eye pain or vision problems, or jaw pain when chewing and a tender scalp happens when you have a weakened immune system or a history of cancer In pregnancy or after giving birth , a severe headache with vision problems, pain below the ribs or sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet can be a sign of pre-eclampsia. Contact your clinic or go to hospital straight away. High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms. It is only very high blood pressure, around 180/120 or above, that can cause a headache, and that is an emergency. See our guide to checking your blood pressure . Headaches are common in children, often from tiredness, stress, missed meals or a viral illness. Migraine in children may be shorter, and some children with migraine have tummy pain more than headache. See a doctor promptly if a child’s headache wakes them up or is there when they wake, keeps getting worse, comes with vomiting or a squint, or follows a head injury. Never give aspirin to children under 16. Why do I keep getting headaches? (Punca kerap sakit kepala) Common causes are stress, poor sleep, skipped meals, dehydration, posture, screen time, eyesight problems and alcohol. Taking painkillers too often can also cause frequent headaches. A headache diary helps find your triggers. What causes headaches at the back of the head near the neck? Usually tension-type headaches or neck problems, often from stress and posture. Sharp, shooting pains from the base of the skull may be occipital neuralgia. See a doctor after an injury or if there are warning signs. How do I get rid of a headache quickly? (Cara hilangkan sakit kepala) Take paracetamol or ibuprofen early, drink water, eat if you’ve missed a meal, and rest. For migraine, a quiet, dark room helps. Menthol or peppermint balms may ease tension headaches. What are the symptoms of migraine? (Simptom migrain) A moderate to severe, throbbing headache, often on one side, lasting 4 hours to 3 days, with nausea or vomiting and sensitivity to light and sound. Some people see flashing lights or zigzags (aura) beforehand. What is a cluster headache? A very severe, one-sided headache around the eye, lasting 15 minutes to 3 hours, with a red, watery eye or runny nose on the same side. Attacks come in clusters over weeks or months, and are much more common in men. Ordinary painkillers don’t help, so see a doctor. When is a headache dangerous? Call 999 for a sudden, extremely severe headache, or a headache with weakness, confusion, slurred speech, a stiff neck and fever, a seizure, or after a head injury. See a doctor urgently for a new or worsening headache.

title: Acne (jerawat): causes, what spots in different places mean, and treatments that work
desc: About two in three Malaysian teenagers get acne, and many adults do too. What causes it, why spots on the back or around the mouth may not be acne at all, which treatments work, and why to avoid creams with hidden steroids.
headings: What causes acne? · Spots in different places: what they can mean · Acne treatments that work · Do acne patches work? · What not to do · Dark marks and scars · When to see a doctor
keywords: Aesthetics & skin Acne (jerawat) Acne vulgaris Jerawat mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Acne is caused by oily skin, blocked pores, skin bacteria and inflammation, often driven by hormones. It isn’t caused by dirt, and scrubbing makes it worse. Itchy, uniform bumps on the back and chest are often “fungal acne” (Malassezia folliculitis), which is common in hot, humid weather and needs antifungal treatment. A rash of small bumps around the mouth may be perioral dermatitis, often triggered by steroid creams, not acne. Benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids and azelaic acid work, but take 8 to 12 weeks. Doctors can add antibiotics, hormonal treatment or isotretinoin. Avoid unregistered creams: NPRA has cancelled products containing hidden steroids, tretinoin and mercury. Acne starts in the hair follicles (pores). Four things work together: The skin makes too much oil (sebum), often driven by hormones during puberty, periods, pregnancy or conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) Dead skin cells block the pores, forming blackheads and whiteheads Bacteria that normally live on the skin ( Cutibacterium acnes ) multiply in the blocked pore Inflammation turns blocked pores into red spots, pus-filled spots, and deeper nodules or cysts Malaysia’s 2022 acne guidelines report acne in about two-thirds of teenagers aged 13 to 17. It usually improves after the teenage years, but adult acne is common, especially in women. What makes it worse: stress, picking or squeezing spots, oily cosmetics and hair products, and possibly high-sugar diets and large amounts of milk (the evidence is limited). Acne isn’t caused by dirty skin. The evidence on chocolate is mixed. Where What it may be Forehead, hairline, eyebrows Acne, often aggravated by oily hair, fringes and hair products. Spots from hair products can take 4 to 6 weeks to clear after stopping the product. Around the mouth, lips and nose Often perioral dermatitis : small red bumps that spare the skin right next to the lip. It is commonly triggered by steroid creams, or inhaled and nasal steroids, and can flare when they are stopped. It needs different treatment from acne. Jawline and chin in adult women Often linked to hormones. Acne with irregular periods or excess hair can be a sign of PCOS. Upper back and chest Acne, or “fungal acne” (Malassezia folliculitis): small, uniform, itchy bumps without blackheads, common in hot, humid weather and in young men. It is treated with antifungal washes or tablets, not acne creams. Buttocks Usually folliculitis (inflamed hair follicles) from sweat, friction and tight clothing, rather than true acne “Face mapping”, the idea that spots in certain areas reflect problems with particular organs, has no scientific basis. A doctor can tell acne apart from look-alikes such as perioral dermatitis and fungal acne. These treatments are recommended in Malaysian and international guidelines: Benzoyl peroxide: kills acne bacteria and reduces inflammation. Available from pharmacies. It can bleach fabrics and cause dryness, so start with a low strength. Topical retinoids (adapalene, tretinoin): unblock pores and prevent new spots. They cause dryness at first, make the skin sensitive to sun, and must not be used in pregnancy. Azelaic acid: treats spots and helps fade dark marks left by acne. Salicylic acid: sold over the counter, with modest benefit for mild acne. Topical antibiotics (clindamycin): prescribed, and always used with benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid, never alone, to prevent resistance.
