If a spot is itchy, calamine can be used on unbroken skin only, never in the mouth or on burst blisters. Ask a doctor first for children under 2. Can adults get HFMD? Yes. Adults can catch HFMD, often from their children, though symptoms are usually milder. You can also get it more than once, because different viruses cause it. Is there a vaccine for HFMD in Malaysia? No. Vaccines against enterovirus 71 are used in China, and one is under review in Malaysia, but they don’t protect against the other viruses that cause most HFMD.

title: Cough that won’t go away? Common causes, cough medicine that helps, and when to see a doctor
desc: After the haze and flu season, many Malaysians have a cough that lingers for weeks. What usually causes it, which cough medicines actually help, safe fever medicine for children, and the signs that need a doctor.
headings: How long is too long for a cough? · Why won’t my cough go away? · Could it be tuberculosis? · Whooping cough in babies · Which cough medicine works? · Home remedies that help · Fever medicine for children · When to see a doctor
keywords: Prevention Cough that won’t go away Cough Batuk denggi aedes nyamuk mosquito jerebu api ipu air pollutant index smoke kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal vaksin suntikan jab immunisation kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Most coughs after a cold or flu clear within 3 to 4 weeks. A cough lasting more than 3 weeks is worth getting checked. Common causes of a lingering cough include a recent infection, haze, allergies, asthma, acid reflux, smoking and some blood pressure medicines. In Malaysia, a cough lasting more than 2 weeks, especially with fever, night sweats or weight loss, should be checked for tuberculosis. Cough syrups have little evidence behind them. Honey (not for babies under 1) and warm drinks are reasonable first steps. Cough and cold medicines should not be used in children under 2 in Malaysia. For fever in children, use paracetamol by weight, and avoid ibuprofen if dengue is possible. Type How long it lasts (adults) Usual cause Acute cough Less than 3 weeks A cold, flu or other infection Subacute cough 3 to 8 weeks Often a cough that lingers after an infection Chronic cough More than 8 weeks Asthma, allergies, reflux, smoking, medicines or lung disease The NHS says a cough usually clears up within 3 to 4 weeks , and advises seeing a doctor if it lasts longer than 3 weeks. In children, US and Australian guidelines treat a cough lasting more than 4 weeks as chronic. 2026 has been hard on Malaysian lungs. Haze pushed air quality into the unhealthy range for weeks, and in the first week of October the Ministry of Health recorded a 10.4% rise in respiratory infections. Flu also circulates all year. Both can leave airways irritated long after the main illness has passed. After a cold or flu: the most common cause. The airways stay sensitive for weeks, causing a dry, tickly cough that slowly fades. Haze and air pollution: fine particles irritate the airways and can trigger coughing, especially in people with asthma. Allergies and post-nasal drip: mucus dripping down the back of the throat from a runny or blocked nose. Often worse at night or in the morning. Asthma: sometimes the only symptom is a cough, especially at night, after exercise or in cold air. Acid reflux: stomach acid irritating the throat. There may be heartburn or a sour taste, but not always. Smoking and vaping: a daily cough is a warning sign of lung damage. Blood pressure medicines: ACE inhibitors, common blood pressure pills whose names usually end in “-pril” (such as perindopril), cause a dry cough in about 1 in 10 people or more. It usually goes about a week after stopping. Don’t stop your medicine yourself. Ask your doctor about switching. Infections that need treatment: such as whooping cough (pertussis) or tuberculosis (see below). Rarely, lung cancer: a cough is rarely a sign of cancer, but it is more likely in smokers and people over 40. Some common blood pressure tablets cause a dry, lingering cough. Your doctor can switch you to another type. Tuberculosis (TB) is still common in Malaysia. In 2024 there were 26,183 cases and 2,580 deaths , according to the Ministry of Health, and more than 3,100 cases were reported in the first six weeks of 2026. The Ministry advises getting checked if you have: a cough lasting more than 2 weeks fever, especially in the evening, or night sweats loss of appetite or weight loss coughing up blood TB is curable with a course of antibiotics, usually for 6 months, and 85–90% of patients are treated successfully. Diagnosis and treatment at government health facilities are heavily subsidised. Getting tested early also protects your family, because TB spreads through the air. Whooping cough (pertussis) causes long coughing fits, sometimes followed by a “whoop” as the child breathes in, or vomiting. It is most dangerous for young babies , who may not whoop at all but stop breathing or turn blue. In 2023, Malaysia recorded 343 cases and 24 deaths by late August, mostly in babies under 5 months old. Babies are protected by the vaccines in the National Immunisation Programme, and by vaccinating mothers during pregnancy. The government announced free whooping cough (Tdap) vaccination for pregnant women from 2024. Ask at your antenatal clinic. Cough medicines are some of the most popular products at any pharmacy, but there is little good evidence that over-the-counter cough syrups help. A Cochrane review of 29 trials found no good evidence for or against them. If you want to try one: Chesty cough with phlegm (batuk berkahak): expectorants such as guaifenesin are meant to loosen mucus. UK guidance lists them as an option for adults and children aged 12 and over, but the evidence is limited. Dry, tickly cough: cough suppressants such as dextromethorphan, for ages 12 and over. Not for a chesty cough, where you need to clear the phlegm. Allergy-related cough: antihistamines such as loratadine may help only when allergies or post-nasal drip are the cause. They don’t help an ordinary post-viral cough. Malaysian rules to know: Cough and cold medicines must carry a warning that they should not be used in children under 2 . Cough mixtures containing codeine and other controlled ingredients can only be supplied by a doctor or pharmacist. In 2023, the Ministry of Health cancelled the registration of all cough products containing pholcodine because of a risk of severe allergic reactions during anaesthesia. Only buy products with a MAL registration number . Unregistered cough syrups sold elsewhere in the region have been contaminated with toxic chemicals. Antibiotics don’t help a cough caused by a virus. A doctor will prescribe them only if a bacterial infection is likely. Honey: a Cochrane review found honey probably eases coughing and helps children sleep. Try 1 to 2 teaspoons in warm water with lemon. Never give honey to babies under 1 , because of the risk of infant botulism. Warm drinks and plenty of fluids soothe the throat and thin mucus. Don’t give hot drinks to small children. Rest , and keep away from cigarette smoke, vapes and smoky kitchens. On hazy days, keep windows closed and use an air purifier if you have one. See our haze guide . Coughs in children often come with fever. For fever medicine (ubat demam budak): Paracetamol can be used from 2 months of age (if born after 37 weeks and over 4 kg). The dose depends on the child’s weight , so check the label or ask a pharmacist. Leave at least 4 hours between doses, give no more than 4 doses in 24 hours, and don’t combine it with other products that also contain paracetamol. Ibuprofen can be used from 3 months and over 5 kg, but avoid it if dengue is possible , because it increases the risk of bleeding. With dengue so common in Malaysia, paracetamol is the safer first choice for fever. Ibuprofen may also be unsuitable for children with asthma or who are dehydrated. Never give aspirin to children under 16. See a doctor if a baby under 3 months has a fever, or if any child with fever seems very unwell, drowsy or dehydrated. See our guide to dengue warning signs . See a GP if: your cough has lasted more than 3 weeks , or more than 2 weeks with fever, night sweats or weight loss you have lost weight without trying you have a weakened immune system or a long-term condition such as diabetes you are over 40 and smoke or used to smoke , and have a new or changed cough your child has had a cough for more than 4 weeks, or has coughing fits with a “whoop” or vomiting Get urgent help or call 999 for Coughing up blood Difficulty breathing, or chest pain Blue or grey lips or skin A baby who stops breathing, turns blue during coughing fits, or is under 6 months with whooping cough symptoms A swollen, painful neck, or a cough that is getting worse very quickly Why won’t my cough go away? (Kenapa batuk berpanjangan?) The most common reason is airways that stay irritated after a cold or flu, which can take 3 to 4 weeks to settle. Other causes include haze, allergies, asthma, acid reflux, smoking and some blood pressure medicines. A cough lasting more than 3 weeks, or 2 weeks with fever or weight loss, should be checked. What is the best cough medicine for adults with phlegm? (Ubat batuk kahak dewasa) Expectorants such as guaifenesin are meant to loosen phlegm, but the evidence is limited. Drinking plenty of fluids and honey in warm water also help. See a doctor if the phlegm is bloody, or the cough lasts more than 3 weeks. How can I get rid of a cough at home? (Petua hilangkan batuk) Try honey with warm water and lemon, plenty of fluids, rest, and avoiding smoke. Don’t give honey to babies under 1. Most coughs clear on their own within a few weeks. When should I worry about a cough? See a doctor for a cough lasting more than 3 weeks, or more than 2 weeks with fever, night sweats or weight loss. Get urgent help for coughing up blood, difficulty breathing, chest pain or blue lips. Can I give cough syrup to my baby? No. In Malaysia, cough and cold medicines carry a warning not to use them in children under 2. Honey should not be given to babies under 1. See a doctor if a baby has a cough with fever or breathing difficulty. What fever medicine is safe for children? (Ubat demam budak) Paracetamol, dosed by the child’s weight, from 2 months of age. Ibuprofen can be used from 3 months but should be avoided if dengue is possible. Never give aspirin to children under 16.

title: Influenza A in Malaysia: symptoms, how long it lasts, A vs B, and when you need antiviral medicine
desc: Influenza A clusters keep closing classrooms in Malaysia. How to tell flu from a cold, how long it lasts and stays contagious, A vs B, who needs antiviral medicine, and the warning signs in children.
headings: Influenza A in Malaysia · What is the difference between influenza A and B? · Symptoms: flu or a cold? · How long does influenza A last, and is it contagious? · Treating flu at home · Antiviral medicine for influenza · Warning signs that need urgent care · Preventing influenza A
keywords: Prevention Influenza A in Malaysia Influenza Demam influenza kencing manis gula hba1c mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal vaksin suntikan jab immunisation kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp
body: Influenza A is the type of flu virus behind most outbreaks and all flu pandemics. Influenza B usually spreads more slowly but is not always milder, especially in children. Symptoms start about 2 days after infection, usually suddenly: fever or chills, cough, sore throat, body aches, headache and tiredness. You are contagious from a day before symptoms start until about 5–7 days after, and longer in young children. Most people recover within a few days to two weeks with rest, fluids and paracetamol. Antibiotics don’t work against flu. Antiviral medicine works best within 48 hours and is mainly for high-risk people: young children, older adults, pregnant women and anyone with a long-term illness. Flu circulates all year round in Malaysia, with surges that are often reported around mid-year and from November to January. Schools and kindergartens are where clusters most often start. October 2025: flu clusters jumped from 14 to 97 in a single week. About 85% were in schools and kindergartens, and around 6,000 students fell ill. By November, 95.6% of samples tested were influenza A (H3). Early 2026: the Ministry of Health’s epidemiology bulletin reported that outbreaks of influenza-like illness in the first 12 weeks of 2026 were 350% higher than in the same period of 2025. September 2026: an influenza A cluster at a boarding school in Ipoh left 46 students with flu-like illness. All were reported stable. The Ministry advises parents to check children for fever, runny nose or cough before school, and to keep them at home and seek treatment if they have symptoms. Influenza A Influenza B Who it infects People, birds and other animals Mainly people Types Subtypes such as H1N1 and H3N2 One main lineage, B/Victoria How it changes Changes quickly; the only type that causes pandemics Changes more slowly Outbreaks Causes most large outbreaks Smaller outbreaks, often in children Covered by the vaccine? Yes, two A strains Yes, one B strain Is influenza A worse than B? Influenza A causes more large outbreaks and often hits older adults hard. But influenza B is not necessarily milder. In children it can be just as severe, and in one US study about a third of children who died from flu had influenza B. The symptoms are the same, and only a lab or rapid test can tell them apart. Treatment is the same for both. Flu usually starts suddenly , often within hours. A cold comes on gradually and is milder. Symptom Flu Common cold Onset Sudden Gradual Fever or chills Common, often high Rare or mild Body aches and tiredness Common, often severe Mild Cough and sore throat Common Common Runny or blocked nose Sometimes Common Headache Common Uncommon Not everyone with flu has a fever. Children are more likely to have vomiting or diarrhoea, and very young children may just seem unusually sleepy, irritable or off their food. Flu usually hits suddenly, with fever, aches and exhaustion, while a cold builds up slowly. Incubation: symptoms usually start about 2 days after you catch the virus, but anywhere from 1 to 4 days. Contagious period: from about 1 day before symptoms start until 5–7 days after. You are most contagious in the first 3 days. Young children and people with weak immune systems can spread it for longer. How long it lasts: most people feel better within a few days to two weeks. Fever usually settles first. A cough and tiredness can linger for a week or two after that. See our guide to a cough that won’t go away . Yes, influenza A is very contagious . It spreads through droplets when people cough, sneeze or talk, and from hands that touch contaminated surfaces. Stay home while you have a fever, and wear a mask around others if you must go out. When can children go back to school? The US CDC advises returning to normal activities once symptoms have been improving and the fever has been gone for at least 24 hours without fever medicine. Ask your doctor for a medical certificate if your child needs one. Rest and stay home from work or school. Drink plenty of fluids : water, clear soups or oral rehydration salts, especially if there is vomiting or diarrhoea. Paracetamol for fever and aches, at the dose on the label for the person’s age and weight. Don’t give aspirin to anyone under 16. It is linked to Reye’s syndrome, a rare but serious illness. Antibiotics don’t work against flu, which is caused by a virus. Your doctor may prescribe them only if a bacterial infection develops, such as some pneumonias or ear infections. If you aren’t improving after a week, or you start to feel better and then get worse again, see a doctor. Antiviral medicines attack the flu virus itself. In Malaysia, they include oseltamivir , taken as capsules or liquid for 5 days, and baloxavir , a single dose for people aged 12 and over. Both need a doctor’s prescription. They work best when started within 48 hours of symptoms starting. In otherwise healthy people, they shorten the illness by about a day. The bigger benefit is lowering the risk of complications in people at high risk. The most common side effect of oseltamivir is nausea or vomiting. Taking it with food helps. Doctors mainly recommend antivirals for people who are very ill or at higher risk of complications: Children under 5, especially under 2 Adults aged 65 and over Pregnant women People with asthma or other lung disease, diabetes, heart disease, kidney or liver disease, or a weakened immune system Most healthy adults and older children with mild flu recover without them. If you or your child is in a high-risk group, see a doctor early , rather than waiting to see if it passes. Antivirals at private clinics can be costly, so ask about the price. Go to an emergency department or call 999 if a child has Fast or difficult breathing, or the ribs pulling in with each breath Bluish lips or face Signs of dehydration: no urine for 8 hours, a dry mouth, or no tears when crying Not waking up, not alert, or not interacting A seizure A fever above 40°C that doesn’t come down with medicine, or any fever in a baby under 12 weeks old Fever or cough that gets better, then comes back worse In adults, get urgent care for Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath Pain or pressure in the chest or abdomen that won’t go away Persistent dizziness, confusion, or being hard to wake A seizure, not passing urine, or severe weakness Symptoms that improve, then return worse See our guide to clinic or emergency department if you aren’t sure where to go. Get a yearly flu vaccine. It protects against two influenza A strains (H1N1 and H3N2) and one influenza B strain, and is free for many older adults. See our flu vaccine guide . Wash your hands often with soap and water, and cover coughs and sneezes. Wear a mask if you have symptoms and must be around others. Keep sick children at home , and avoid crowds while you are unwell. What is the difference between influenza A and B? (Apa beza influenza A dan B?) Influenza A infects people and animals, changes quickly and causes most large outbreaks and all pandemics. Influenza B mainly infects people and changes more slowly. The symptoms and treatment are the same, and the yearly vaccine covers both. Is influenza A contagious? Yes, very. You can spread it from about 1 day before symptoms start until 5–7 days after, and young children can spread it for longer. Stay home while you have a fever. How long does influenza A last? (Influenza A berapa lama?) Most people recover within a few days to two weeks. Fever usually settles in a few days, but a cough and tiredness can last a week or two longer. What medicine is used for influenza A? (Ubat influenza A) Most people only need rest, fluids and paracetamol. Doctors may prescribe antiviral medicine such as oseltamivir for people at high risk or who are very ill, ideally within 48 hours of symptoms starting. Antibiotics don’t work against flu. Is influenza A worse than influenza B? Influenza A causes more outbreaks and is often harder on older adults, but influenza B can be just as severe, especially in children. Both should be taken seriously in high-risk people. What are the signs of influenza in children? (Tanda demam influenza kanak-kanak) Sudden fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, aches and tiredness. Children are more likely than adults to have vomiting or diarrhoea. Seek urgent care for fast or difficult breathing, bluish lips, dehydration, a seizure or a fever above 40°C.

title: Stroke or heart attack in Kuala Lumpur: the warning signs, what to do, and where to get treated fast
desc: Heart disease is Malaysia’s leading cause of death, and Malaysians have heart attacks younger than people in many countries. How to spot a stroke or heart attack, what to do in the first minutes, and why time matters so much.
headings: Why minutes matter · Stroke warning signs: BE FAST · Heart attack warning signs · What to do while you wait for help · Ambulance response times · Treatments that depend on time · Hospitals in and around Kuala Lumpur · Lower your risk
keywords: Heart & diabetes Stroke and heart attack in KL Stroke Strok kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp saringan check-up checkup medical
body: Heart disease is Malaysia’s leading cause of death, and stroke is consistently among the top three. Spot a stroke with BE FAST: Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech, Time to call 999. Heart attack signs include chest pain or pressure, pain spreading to the arm, jaw or back, breathlessness and sweating. Women, older people and people with diabetes may have no chest pain. Call 999, or 112 from a mobile, and note the time symptoms started. Clot-busting treatment for stroke must start within 4.5 hours. Don’t give aspirin for a suspected stroke. For a suspected heart attack, take aspirin only if the 999 operator or a doctor tells you to. Ischaemic heart disease is Malaysia’s leading cause of death. It caused 17,421 deaths in 2024, 13% of medically certified deaths, according to the Department of Statistics. Stroke is consistently among the top three causes, and is estimated to affect more than 50,000 Malaysians a year. Malaysians also have heart attacks young. In the national heart registry for 2020–2021, the average age at admission with a heart attack or unstable angina was 58.5 years , and a quarter of patients were under 50. Most strokes and heart attacks are caused by a blocked artery. In a stroke, about 1.9 million brain cells die every minute the blockage continues. Yet in a Malaysian stroke study, patients took a median of seven hours or more to reach hospital, too late for the most effective treatments. A stroke comes on suddenly . Use BE FAST to check, or its Malay version, PeRMATA: BE FAST What to look for PeRMATA B alance Sudden dizziness, loss of balance or trouble walking Pe ning E yes Sudden blurred, double or lost vision R abun F ace One side of the face droops. Ask them to smile. M uka herot A rm Weakness or numbness in one arm or leg. Ask them to raise both arms. A ngkat tangan S peech Slurred speech, or difficulty speaking or understanding T utur T ime Call 999 now, and note the time symptoms started A ngkat telefon Call 999 even if the symptoms go away after a few minutes. This can be a “mini-stroke” (transient ischaemic attack), which is a warning that a major stroke may follow. Chest pain, pressure, tightness or squeezing , lasting more than a few minutes or coming and going Pain spreading to one or both arms, the neck, jaw, back or upper stomach Shortness of breath Cold sweat, nausea or vomiting, or light-headedness Women, older people and people with diabetes are more likely to have a heart attack without obvious chest pain. They may feel only breathlessness, nausea, unusual tiredness or discomfort in the back or jaw. Don’t dismiss these as indigestion or “angin”, especially if you have risk factors. High blood pressure is the main risk factor for both stroke and heart attack, and often has no symptoms. Call 999 (or 112 from a mobile). Say you suspect a stroke or heart attack and give the exact address. Note the time symptoms started, or when the person was last seen well. Doctors need this to decide on treatment. Keep the person still , sitting or lying in a comfortable position, and loosen tight clothing. For a suspected stroke: give nothing to eat or drink, as swallowing may be affected. Don’t give aspirin . Some strokes are caused by bleeding, which aspirin can make worse, and only a brain scan can tell. For a suspected heart attack: take aspirin only if the 999 operator or a doctor tells you to, and not if you are allergic to it. Use your own heart medicines, such as a GTN spray, as your doctor has advised. If the person collapses and isn’t breathing normally, start hands-only CPR: push hard and fast in the centre of the chest, about twice a second, and keep going until help arrives. Ask someone to find an AED (defibrillator) if one is nearby. Gather the person’s IC and a list of their medicines. Don’t go to a GP clinic A GP clinic can’t give clot-busting treatment, and going there first loses precious time. Call 999. If you can’t wait for an ambulance, have someone else drive you straight to a hospital emergency department. Don’t drive yourself. Ambulance response is a known weak spot. In 2025, only 34.01% of the most urgent (Priority 1) cases were reached within the 15-minute target, against a goal of 50%, the Health Minister told Parliament in October 2026. Budget 2027 funds 400 new ambulances for Ministry of Health hospitals. Calling 999 is still the right first step, because it gets trained help on the way. If the ambulance is delayed and the person is stable enough to travel, a family member can drive them to the nearest hospital emergency department. Treatment What it does Time window Thrombolysis (stroke) A clot-busting drug through a drip Within 4.5 hours of symptoms starting Thrombectomy (stroke) A thin tube removes a large clot from a brain artery Best within 6 hours; up to 24 hours in selected patients Primary angioplasty (heart attack) A balloon and stent reopen the blocked heart artery in a cath lab Target: within 90 minutes of arriving at hospital Thrombolysis (heart attack) A clot-busting drug, when angioplasty isn’t quickly available Target: within 30 minutes of arriving at hospital Malaysian hospitals are getting faster. In the national heart registry for 2020–2021, the median time from arrival to angioplasty was 69.5 minutes, and 63.6% of patients were treated within the 90-minute target. The biggest delay is usually before the patient reaches hospital. In an emergency, go to the nearest hospital emergency department, or where the ambulance takes you. Every emergency department can assess you, start treatment and transfer you if a specialist procedure is needed. Stroke: these government and university hospitals in the Klang Valley have stroke units and can perform thrombectomy, according to the international Angels Initiative stroke network: Hospital Kuala Lumpur (HKL) Hospital Sungai Buloh University Malaya Medical Centre (UMMC) Hospital Canselor Tuanku Muhriz (HCTM), UKM, Cheras HCTM and Hospital Sultan Abdul Aziz Shah (UPM) in Serdang are certified as advanced stroke centres by the World Stroke Organization. Heart attack: the National Heart Institute (IJN) runs a 24-hour heart attack centre for emergency angioplasty, and Hospital Serdang has a large cardiac centre. Major university hospitals and many private hospitals in the Klang Valley also have cath labs and stroke services. If you have heart disease or have had a stroke, ask your doctor now which hospital you should go to in an emergency, and save the details in your phone. Most strokes and heart attacks are linked to risk factors you can check and treat. Among Malaysian adults, according to the National Health and Morbidity Survey 2023: 29.2% have high blood pressure , and 11.9% have it without knowing. 15.6% have diabetes and 33.3% have high cholesterol. 19.0% smoke, and 29.9% are physically inactive. Check your blood pressure at least once a year from age 18, and your blood sugar and cholesterol from age 30. Many people qualify for free health screening . You can also check your blood pressure at home . Take medicines as prescribed, stop smoking, and aim for 150 minutes of activity a week. What are the warning signs of a stroke? Use BE FAST: sudden loss of Balance, blurred or lost vision (Eyes), a drooping Face, weakness in one Arm or leg, slurred Speech. Then it’s Time to call 999. In Malay, the same signs are remembered as PeRMATA. Should I give aspirin to someone having a stroke? No. Some strokes are caused by bleeding in the brain, which aspirin can make worse. Only a brain scan can tell the difference, so give nothing by mouth and call 999. Should I take aspirin during a heart attack? Only if the 999 operator or a doctor tells you to, and not if you are allergic to aspirin. Call 999 first. How long do you have to treat a stroke? Clot-busting treatment must start within 4.5 hours of symptoms starting. Removing a large clot (thrombectomy) works best within 6 hours, and up to 24 hours in selected patients. The sooner, the better. Which hospitals in KL treat stroke? Hospital Kuala Lumpur, Hospital Sungai Buloh, University Malaya Medical Centre and Hospital Canselor Tuanku Muhriz (UKM) have stroke units and can remove clots. In an emergency, call 999 and go to the nearest emergency department. Can women have a heart attack without chest pain? Yes. Women, older people and people with diabetes are more likely to have breathlessness, nausea, unusual tiredness or back or jaw discomfort instead of classic chest pain.

title: Thalassaemia screening in Malaysia: who gets free tests, and what a carrier result means
desc: About 1 in 20 Malaysians carries a thalassaemia gene, usually without knowing it. Who can get screened for free, how the test works, and what to do if you or your partner is a carrier.
headings: What is thalassaemia? · How common is it in Malaysia? · How thalassaemia is passed on · What Budget 2027 changes · Who is screened for free · How the test works · Thalassaemia trait or iron deficiency? · If you or your partner is a carrier · Where to get screened in Kuala Lumpur
keywords: Prevention Thalassaemia screening in Malaysia Thalassemia Talasemia mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal klinik doctor doktor gp saringan check-up checkup medical aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Thalassaemia is an inherited blood disorder. Carriers (thalassaemia trait) are healthy and need no treatment, but can pass the gene to their children. About 1 in 20 Malaysians is a carrier. Of more than 920,000 Form 4 students screened between 2017 and 2020, 5.8% were carriers. If both parents are carriers, each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of a child with thalassaemia major. Free screening is offered to Form 4 students, pregnant women and relatives of carriers. Budget 2027 extends it to husbands and children in at-risk carrier families. Screening starts with a full blood count. Small red blood cells (MCV below 80 fL or MCH below 27 pg) lead to a haemoglobin analysis. Thalassaemia is a group of inherited conditions in which the body makes too little normal haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. The main types in Malaysia are alpha thalassaemia , beta thalassaemia and haemoglobin E (HbE) , which can combine with beta thalassaemia. There is a big difference between carrying the gene and having the disease: Carrier (thalassaemia trait or minor): one altered gene. Carriers are healthy, may have slightly small red blood cells or mild anaemia, and need no treatment. Most don’t know they are carriers. Thalassaemia major and other severe forms: two altered genes. Severe forms need blood transfusions every few weeks for life, plus daily medicine to remove the extra iron that transfusions build up in the body. Milder forms may need transfusions only sometimes. Malaysia’s Ministry of Health now groups patients by whether they depend on regular transfusions (transfusion-dependent thalassaemia) or not. Thalassaemia is one of the most common inherited conditions in Malaysia. Between 2017 and 2020, 924,487 Form 4 students were screened, and 53,559 (5.8%) were carriers, about 1 in 17. Rates differ between states and communities. In February 2026, the Health Minister told Parliament that carrier rates were highest in Sabah, Selangor and Kedah. The Malaysian Thalassaemia Registry’s 2023 report lists 9,554 patients treated in public hospitals. Lifelong treatment is expensive: the Health Ministry estimates about RM3 million per patient from infancy to age 40. Screening is working. New thalassaemia births fell by about half between 2009 and 2021, and the national programme aims to cut them by up to 75% by 2030. Everyone has two copies of the genes involved, one from each parent. When both parents are carriers of the same type, each pregnancy has: Chance Child’s result 1 in 4 (25%) Thalassaemia major or another severe form 1 in 2 (50%) Carrier, like the parents 1 in 4 (25%) Not affected and not a carrier These chances are the same for every pregnancy. Having one affected child doesn’t make the next one safer. When only one parent is a carrier , each child has a 1 in 2 chance of being a carrier, but not of having a severe form from those genes. This is why screening matters most for couples planning to marry or have children, and for the family of anyone found to be a carrier. If one family member is a carrier, parents, brothers, sisters and children may be carriers too. Budget 2027, tabled on 9 October 2026, extends free thalassaemia screening by the Ministry of Health to husbands and children in at-risk carrier families , to reduce the number of babies born with thalassaemia major. In practice, this means that if a woman is found to be a carrier, for example during pregnancy, her husband and children can be screened for free. The government has not yet announced a start date or how families will be called for screening. Ask at your Klinik Kesihatan if you think your family qualifies. Form 4 students: the national school programme has offered free screening since 2016, with parents’ written consent. Each student gets a Thalassaemia Screening Card showing their result. Pregnant women: screened as part of antenatal care at government clinics since 2009. Relatives of carriers and patients: parents, brothers, sisters and children (known as cascade screening). From 2027: husbands and children in at-risk carrier families, under Budget 2027. Anyone who asks: government health clinics also offer voluntary screening, including for couples planning to marry. Premarital thalassaemia screening is voluntary in Malaysia, unlike HIV screening for Muslim couples. Keep your screening card or result safely. You only need to be screened once, as your genes don’t change. Full blood count (FBC): a routine blood test. Thalassaemia is suspected if your red blood cells are small, with an MCV below 80 fL or an MCH below 27 pg. Haemoglobin analysis: a laboratory test (HPLC or capillary electrophoresis) that identifies beta thalassaemia, HbE and some other types. DNA analysis: done when needed, mainly to confirm alpha thalassaemia, which a haemoglobin analysis can miss. You don’t usually need to fast. Some types, including mild alpha thalassaemia and HbE, can show normal red cell sizes, so a normal FBC doesn’t always rule out being a carrier. If thalassaemia runs in your family, tell the doctor. Screening starts with a routine full blood count, the same test used in a health check. Both thalassaemia trait and iron deficiency cause small red blood cells, and both are common in Malaysia, so they are easily confused. A doctor can tell them apart with an iron test (ferritin) and a haemoglobin analysis. Don’t start iron tablets just because a blood test shows small red cells or mild anaemia. Iron doesn’t help thalassaemia trait, and extra iron can build up over time. Severe iron deficiency can hide beta thalassaemia trait on the haemoglobin analysis. Your doctor may treat the iron deficiency first and repeat the test, although couples at risk should still be fully tested. You are healthy. Being a carrier doesn’t turn into thalassaemia major, and you don’t need treatment. Tell your family. Your parents, brothers, sisters and children may also be carriers and can be screened. Test your partner before or early in pregnancy. If only one of you is a carrier, your children cannot have a severe form from those genes. If you are both carriers, ask for genetic counselling . A counsellor will explain your options without pressure. These include testing a pregnancy early by chorionic villus sampling (CVS) or amniocentesis, which carry a small risk of miscarriage, or IVF with genetic testing of embryos before pregnancy. Some of the DNA tests are done by private laboratories, so ask about costs. See a doctor if a child has Pale skin, poor feeding or slow growth Unusual tiredness or breathlessness A swollen tummy or yellow eyes Severe thalassaemia usually shows in the first two years of life. Klinik Kesihatan (government health clinics) offer free walk-in, voluntary and family screening. Bring your MyKad, and if you are a relative of a carrier, their screening card or result. Private GP clinics can do a full blood count and send blood for haemoglobin analysis at a private laboratory, for a fee. Children with thalassaemia in Kuala Lumpur are treated at government hospitals, including Hospital Tunku Azizah, which also offers stem cell transplants, the only established cure. Is thalassaemia screening free in Malaysia? Yes, for Form 4 students, pregnant women, relatives of carriers and patients, and anyone who asks at a government health clinic. Budget 2027 extends free screening to husbands and children in at-risk carrier families. How common is thalassaemia in Malaysia? About 1 in 20 Malaysians is a carrier. Among more than 920,000 Form 4 students screened between 2017 and 2020, 5.8% were carriers. What is the difference between thalassaemia minor and major? Thalassaemia minor (trait) means you carry one altered gene. You are healthy and need no treatment. Thalassaemia major means two altered genes and usually needs regular blood transfusions for life. If both parents are thalassaemia carriers, will the baby have it? Not necessarily. Each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of thalassaemia major, a 1 in 2 chance of being a carrier, and a 1 in 4 chance of being unaffected. Genetic counselling can explain your options. Which blood test detects thalassaemia? Screening starts with a full blood count. If the red cells are small (MCV below 80 fL or MCH below 27 pg), a haemoglobin analysis follows, and sometimes DNA analysis for alpha thalassaemia. Is premarital thalassaemia screening compulsory in Malaysia? No. Premarital thalassaemia screening is voluntary, although it is strongly encouraged. HIV screening is the premarital test that is compulsory for Muslim couples.

title: Budget 2027 and your health: what changes for patients in Kuala Lumpur
desc: Budget 2027 gives the Health Ministry RM47.7 billion. What actually changes for patients in KL: medical bills, insurance, screening, waiting times, elderly care and tax relief.
headings: Budget 2027 health measures at a glance · Help with paying for treatment · MediAsas and private hospital bills · Shorter waits at government hospitals · Screening, fertility and vaccines · Elderly care · What it means for Kuala Lumpur · Tax relief changes for 2027 · What you can do now
keywords: Guides Budget 2027 and your health mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal vaksin suntikan jab immunisation kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp saringan check-up checkup medical
body: The Health Ministry’s budget rises to RM47.7 billion in 2027, up from RM46.5 billion. MediAsas, an affordable basic medical insurance plan, launches in January 2027. EPF members under 55 can pay for it from Akaun Sejahtera. The Medical Assistance Fund for people who can’t afford treatment grows from RM40 million to RM60 million. PeKa B40 continues with RM80 million. Free thalassaemia screening is extended to the husbands and children of carriers. Two DBKL buildings in Taman Desa and Cheras will become senior daycare centres, and service tax on elderly care falls from 8% to 6%. The Madani Medical Scheme for minor illnesses at private GP clinics has no allocation in the 2027 estimates. Budget 2027 was tabled on 9 October 2026. These are the measures most likely to affect patients and families: Measure What it means for you MediAsas Basic medical insurance or takaful from January 2027, payable from EPF Akaun Sejahtera Medical Assistance Fund RM60 million (from RM40 million) for patients who can’t afford treatment PeKa B40 RM80 million for free screening and treatment support for STR recipients aged 40+ Thalassaemia screening Free for husbands and children of carriers Outsourcing to private hospitals RM200 million to send government patients to other facilities and shorten waits Private hospital bills Standard, transparent charge categories from 2027 Elderly care Service tax cut from 8% to 6%; two new senior daycare centres in KL Tax relief Medical relief extended to postnatal care; parents’ relief covers all care costs Most of these take effect in 2027. Tax changes still need to be passed in the Finance Bill. Medical Assistance Fund (Tabung Bantuan Perubatan): increased from RM40 million to RM60 million. It helps patients at government hospitals who can’t afford treatment or medical devices. Ask the hospital’s medical social work unit how to apply. PeKa B40: RM80 million, the same as in 2026. Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR) recipients aged 40 and above, and their spouses, get free health screening, help with medical devices, and incentives to complete cancer treatment. Eligibility is automatic. MySalam: the free takaful protection scheme for lower-income Malaysians continues in 2027. Care aid for bedridden patients: the monthly aid for bedridden persons with disabilities and chronically ill patients rises from RM500 to RM600. The Madani Medical Scheme The Madani Medical Scheme (Skim Perubatan Madani) subsidised visits to private GP clinics for minor illnesses such as fever, diarrhoea and headaches for lower-income Malaysians. Its funding was halved to RM50 million in 2026, and CodeBlue reports it has no allocation in the Health Ministry’s 2027 estimates. The government has not announced an end date. If you rely on it, ask your clinic whether it is still accepting the scheme. Government health clinics (Klinik Kesihatan) remain a low-cost option for minor illnesses. MediAsas is a basic medical insurance and takaful plan that launches in January 2027 . It is designed to be affordable for people who have no medical cover or have dropped a plan they could no longer pay for. Under Budget 2027: EPF members under 55 can pay MediAsas premiums from their Akaun Sejahtera . Companies with fewer than 75 staff get a RM200 subsidy for each employee’s first-year premium, for up to 50 employees. About 200,000 workers are expected to benefit. Hospitals will be paid by diagnosis and type of treatment (Diagnosis Related Groups), which aims to make costs more predictable. Separately, from 2027 private hospitals must use standard, transparent charge categories on their bills, so patients can see and compare what they are paying for. See our full guide: MediAsas explained: cover, premiums and who it suits . Outsourcing to other facilities: the allocation for sending government patients elsewhere rises to RM200 million. It now includes using private facilities, including operating theatres, and covers expanded newborn screening, prenatal genetic tests and rehabilitation. More specialists: retired government specialists and private specialists can work sessions at government hospitals on more flexible terms and for longer. More permanent doctors: more than 9,000 contract doctors will be offered permanent posts in 2027. The monthly incentive for about 47,000 nurses and paramedics with post-basic training doubles from RM100 to RM200. Ambulances and equipment: more than RM770 million for medical equipment, including 400 new ambulances and upgraded haemodialysis facilities. The new ambulances matter. In 2025, only about a third of the most urgent emergency calls were reached within the 15-minute target. In an emergency, always call 999 . If you are unsure whether you need an ambulance, see our guide to clinic or emergency department . Thalassaemia: free screening at Ministry of Health facilities is extended to the husbands and children of carriers . Thalassaemia is an inherited blood disorder. Two carriers have a 1 in 4 chance in each pregnancy of having a child with thalassaemia major, who needs lifelong blood transfusions. Screening helps couples know their risk. See our thalassaemia screening guide . Fertility (BuAi programme): subsidised fertility treatment (intrauterine insemination) for 2,000 couples through LPPKN, and men’s wellness services for 42,000 people. HPV vaccine: the school programme for about 230,000 Year 6 girls moves to a vaccine that covers nine HPV types instead of two. See our HPV vaccine guide . Drivers: commercial vehicle drivers get PERKESO health screening vouchers worth up to RM30. Mobile clinics: 10 university teaching hospitals will run screening and mobile clinics for lower-income, vulnerable and rural communities. For free screening you can already use, see free health screening in Malaysia 2026 . Service tax on elderly care falls from 8% to 6% from 1 January 2027, and care fees of up to RM96,000 a year are fully exempt from service tax. Two senior daycare centres in Kuala Lumpur: two DBKL buildings, at the Anjung Kelana homeless transformation centre in Taman Desa and the Cheras temporary market, will be upgraded into senior daycare centres. Opening dates have not been announced. Getting around KL: 22 km of covered walkways, including links from homes to clinics, and buggies for older visitors at Tugu Negara, the Perdana Botanical Gardens and Carcosa. Bantuan Warga Emas: RM1.3 billion for about 200,000 recipients. A Senior Citizens Bill is also planned. Budget 2027 extends tax relief to all care costs for parents and grandparents, not only medical bills. None of the four new health facilities named in the budget speech are in Kuala Lumpur. They are in Johor, Kuching, Gerik and Rembau. For KL residents, the most visible changes are likely to be: Hospital Kuala Lumpur (HKL) is one of 16 hospitals rolling out a full Hospital Information System in 2027, with RM200 million for the initiative. HKL’s director said the aim is a fully computerised hospital, so patients don’t have to repeat their medical history at every stage of care. Lift replacement is under way, and electrical and IT upgrades are planned. Linked medical records: a separate RM1 billion investment by the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) will connect electronic records across 150 hospitals and 2,488 health clinics under a “one person, one record” approach, with telehealth services. Repairs and air-conditioning: RM1.2 billion for maintaining public hospitals and clinics nationwide, including new air-conditioning at 600 Ministry of Health clinic facilities. The two senior daycare centres in Taman Desa and Cheras, and new covered walkways. These apply from the 2027 year of assessment, once passed in the Finance Bill: Medical expenses relief is extended to postnatal care . News reports say the overall limit stays at RM10,000, with postnatal care capped at RM3,000 within it. Vaccinations, health screening, dental treatment and fertility treatment remain claimable. Relief for parents and grandparents now covers all care expenses, not only medical treatment. Individual relief rises from RM9,000 to RM12,000. Keep receipts for medical, screening, vaccination and care expenses. Check the final rules with LHDN before filing. If you are 40 or over, check whether you qualify for free screening through PeKa B40 or PERKESO, and book it before the year ends. If you have no medical insurance, or are struggling with premiums, compare your current plan with MediAsas when insurers publish prices. Don’t cancel an existing policy until new cover is in place. If thalassaemia runs in your family, ask your Klinik Kesihatan about free screening for your spouse and children. If you care for an older parent, keep receipts for care costs, which can be claimed under the expanded relief from 2027. How much does the Health Ministry get in Budget 2027? RM47.7 billion, up from about RM46.5 billion in 2026, an increase of RM1.18 billion. When does MediAsas start? January 2027. EPF members under 55 can pay MediAsas premiums from their Akaun Sejahtera, and small companies get a RM200 subsidy per employee for the first year. Who can get free thalassaemia screening under Budget 2027? Free screening at Ministry of Health facilities is extended to the husbands and children of thalassaemia carriers. Ask at your nearest Klinik Kesihatan. Is the Madani Medical Scheme continuing in 2027? CodeBlue reports that the scheme has no allocation in the Health Ministry’s 2027 estimates, after its funding was halved in 2026. No end date has been announced, so check with your clinic. Are there new senior daycare centres in Kuala Lumpur? Yes. Two DBKL buildings, in Taman Desa and at the Cheras temporary market, will be upgraded into senior daycare centres. Opening dates have not been announced. What medical tax relief changes in 2027? Medical expenses relief is extended to postnatal care, and parents’ relief covers all care expenses, not only medical bills. These still need to be passed in the Finance Bill.

title: MediAsas explained: Malaysia’s basic medical insurance plan from January 2027
desc: MediAsas is a basic medical insurance and takaful plan launching in January 2027. Teras and Fleksi compared, what it covers, the main exclusions, expected premiums and who it suits.
headings: Why MediAsas was created · Teras and Fleksi: the two plans · What MediAsas covers · What it doesn’t cover · Who can buy it · How much will it cost? · How hospitals are paid, and why it matters · Should you get MediAsas?
keywords: Guides MediAsas explained denggi aedes nyamuk mosquito mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: MediAsas is a standardised basic medical insurance and takaful plan backed by Bank Negara Malaysia and the Ministry of Finance. It launches nationwide in January 2027. There are two versions: Teras, with an annual limit of RM100,000 (RM150,000 from age 60) and a small deductible, and Fleksi, with a RM300,000 limit and a RM10,000 deductible, meant to top up employer cover. It is voluntary and fully underwritten. Pre-existing conditions are not covered, and there are 35 main exclusions. Final premiums have not been published. The government has indicated about RM60 to RM550 a month, depending on age. EPF members under 55 can pay premiums from Akaun Sejahtera. Don’t cancel an existing plan until new cover is in place. Medical costs in Malaysia rose about 15% in 2024, and many insurers raised premiums sharply. Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) stepped in with interim measures in December 2024, asking insurers to spread increases over at least three years. Even so, about 340,000 medical policies were surrendered between January 2024 and June 2025, according to BNM’s white paper on medical insurance. MediAsas, first called the “Base MHIT plan”, is the result. It is a simple, standard plan, the same at every provider, with cost-sharing and hospital payment rules designed to keep premiums affordable over the long term. MediAsas comes in two versions, each offered as conventional insurance or as takaful. These figures are from BNM’s pilot programme. BNM says benefits may change in the final version launched in January 2027. MediAsas Teras MediAsas Fleksi Who it is for People with no other medical cover People with employer or other cover who want protection for large bills Annual limit RM100,000 (RM150,000 from age 60) RM300,000 Lifetime limit None None Deductible RM500 per illness or injury (RM1,000 from age 60) at network hospitals RM10,000 a year at network hospitals, RM15,000 elsewhere Outside the hospital network Deductible plus 20% co-payment, capped at RM3,000 Higher deductible No deductible for Government hospitals, emergencies and outpatient cancer treatment No waivers A deductible is the amount you pay yourself before the plan pays. A co-payment is a share of the bill you pay on top. Both help keep premiums lower. Hospital stays: a shared room (two or four beds), intensive care, surgery and day surgery, and ambulance. You can upgrade to a single room, but you pay the difference. Before and after hospital: tests and consultations up to 30 days before admission and 90 days after, including physiotherapy, home nursing and the GP visit that referred you. Cancer: outpatient cancer treatment such as chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Some outpatient care at hospitals: dengue, influenza, bronchitis and pneumonia, up to RM3,000 a year. It does not cover treatment overseas, and there is no no-claim bonus. MediAsas also pays for the GP visit that refers you to hospital, and for follow-up after discharge. BNM lists 35 main exclusions. The most important are: Pre-existing conditions , and congenital or hereditary conditions Mental and nervous disorders Pregnancy, childbirth and fertility treatment Dental treatment, spectacles and eye surgery to correct vision Cosmetic surgery and weight management Implanted devices such as pacemakers and hearing aids Sexually transmitted infections, including HIV Self-harm, substance misuse and hazardous sports There is also a 30-day waiting period for illness (accidents are covered straight away) and a 120-day waiting period for specified illnesses. Read the full list of exclusions in the policy before you buy. Age: you can join from birth up to age 70, and renew each year up to age 85. Residency: the pilot was limited to Malaysian citizens. BNM says permanent residents and foreigners living in Malaysia will be able to join at the national launch. Health questions: MediAsas is fully underwritten. You must answer a health questionnaire honestly, and the insurer can decline you, charge more, or exclude a condition. BNM has said some well-managed conditions may be accepted. One plan only: you can hold only one MediAsas policy at a time. If you cancel it, you must go through underwriting again to rejoin. If you didn’t disclose something by mistake, the insurer can’t dispute a claim on that basis after seven years, except for fraud, deliberate non-disclosure, or major illnesses such as cancer, organ failure and serious heart disease that existed before cover started. Final premiums have not been published. The government has indicated a range of about RM60 to RM550 a month , depending on your age when you join, with the lowest premiums for younger people. Insurers will publish prices closer to the January 2027 launch. Premiums are not guaranteed. They rise as you get older, and can be reviewed for everyone in the plan based on how the whole MediAsas pool performs, with at least 30 days’ written notice. Your premium does not go up just because you made a claim. BNM plans an independent governance board to review prices each year. Ways to pay under Budget 2027: EPF members under 55 can pay premiums from Akaun Sejahtera (Account 2). Companies with fewer than 75 staff get RM200 off each employee’s first-year premium , for up to 50 employees. How employers claim this has not yet been announced. Premiums may also qualify for income tax relief on medical insurance, subject to LHDN’s rules. MediAsas network hospitals are paid a set amount for each type of diagnosis and treatment, known as Diagnosis Related Groups (DRG) , instead of item by item. This aims to stop costs rising unpredictably, which keeps premiums stable. For you, the deductible and limits stay the same. BNM’s example: a hospital stay for food poisoning billed at RM12,000 might be paid at RM10,000 under DRG. Separately, Budget 2027 requires all private hospitals to use standard, transparent charge categories on bills from 2027. You have no medical cover: Teras is designed for you. Compare prices when they are published in early 2027. You only have employer cover: employer plans usually end when you leave the job and may have low limits. Fleksi is designed to sit on top for large bills. You already have a personal plan: BNM says MediAsas is meant to complement existing cover, not replace it. Compare limits, room and board, exclusions and premiums carefully. Your current plan may cover conditions MediAsas excludes, especially if you have developed a condition since you bought it. You are on a low income: PeKa B40 and MySalam already give free protection to eligible Malaysians. Government hospitals remain heavily subsidised. Don’t cancel your current plan first If you cancel an existing policy, any condition you have developed since it started is likely to count as pre-existing under MediAsas and won’t be covered. Only change plans once new cover has been approved and you have compared what you would lose. When does MediAsas start? MediAsas launches nationwide in January 2027. A pilot with six insurers and takaful operators and 10 private hospitals ran in the Klang Valley from July 2026. How much is MediAsas a month? Final premiums have not been published. The government has indicated about RM60 to RM550 a month, depending on your age when you join. What is the difference between MediAsas Teras and Fleksi? Teras is a basic plan with an annual limit of RM100,000 (RM150,000 from age 60) and a deductible of RM500 per illness at network hospitals. Fleksi has a RM300,000 limit and a RM10,000 yearly deductible, and is meant to top up employer cover. Does MediAsas cover pre-existing conditions? No. MediAsas is fully underwritten and excludes pre-existing conditions. Some well-managed conditions may be accepted at the insurer’s discretion. Can I use EPF to pay for MediAsas? Yes, if you are under 55. Budget 2027 allows EPF members to pay MediAsas premiums from Akaun Sejahtera. Should I cancel my current medical insurance for MediAsas? Not without comparing carefully and getting new cover approved first. Conditions you developed after buying your current plan would likely be excluded as pre-existing under MediAsas.

title: World Diabetes Day 2026: how and where to get your blood sugar checked in KL
desc: World Diabetes Day falls on Saturday 14 November. Which test to ask for, what the numbers mean under Malaysian guidelines, free ways to get tested in KL, and what to do if you have prediabetes.
headings: This year’s theme: early action · Who should get tested · Which test to ask for · What your results mean · If you have prediabetes · Free and low-cost tests in Kuala Lumpur · When high blood sugar is an emergency
keywords: Heart & diabetes World Diabetes Day 2026 Diabetes mellitus Kencing manis kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp saringan check-up checkup medical
body: World Diabetes Day is on Saturday 14 November 2026. The theme for 2026–27 is “Early action on diabetes”. 15.6% of Malaysian adults have diabetes, and two in five of them don’t know it. Malaysia diagnoses diabetes at an HbA1c of 6.3% or above, lower than the 6.5% used in many other countries. 5.7% to 6.2% is prediabetes. A finger-prick reading is only a first screen. Diabetes is confirmed with a blood test from a vein, usually repeated. Free tests are available at Klinik Kesihatan (book in MySejahtera), through PeKa B40 and PERKESO, and at Diabetes Malaysia’s KL event on 14 November. The International Diabetes Federation has chosen “Early action on diabetes” as the World Diabetes Day theme for 2026 and 2027. It focuses on finding diabetes sooner and lowering the risk for people who don’t have it yet. Globally, about 1 in 9 adults has diabetes, and up to half already have complications by the time they are diagnosed. In Malaysia, the National Health and Morbidity Survey (NHMS) 2023 found diabetes in 15.6% of adults , about 3.6 million people. Two in five didn’t know they had it, and more than half of those who did know didn’t have their blood sugar under control. On 6 October 2026, the Health Minister told Parliament that more than 80% of adults aged 18 to 29 with diabetes are undiagnosed. We covered those figures in undiagnosed diabetes and high blood pressure in young Malaysians . Malaysia’s Clinical Practice Guidelines recommend a blood sugar test for everyone from age 30 , repeated every year if normal. Get tested earlier , at any adult age, if you: have a BMI over 23 (lower than the international overweight cut-off of 25, because Asians tend to develop diabetes at lower weights) have a parent, brother or sister with diabetes had diabetes in pregnancy have polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), heart disease, or abnormal cholesterol are mostly inactive, or take medicines such as long-term steroids If you have prediabetes, you should be tested every year. A finger-prick glucose test is a useful first check, but it can’t diagnose diabetes on its own. Test How it works Fasting? HbA1c Shows your average blood sugar over the last 2–3 months No Fasting plasma glucose Blood sugar after an overnight fast Yes, at least 8 hours Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) Blood sugar before and 2 hours after a 75 g glucose drink Yes; plain water only, rest during the test Finger-prick (capillary) glucose A quick screen with a glucometer Either HbA1c is the most convenient, because you don’t need to fast. It is less reliable if you are anaemic, have kidney disease, take iron supplements or steroids, or have a haemoglobin variant such as thalassaemia trait. Your doctor may use a glucose test instead. A finger-prick test at a pharmacy, event or at home is only a first screen. If it reads 5.6 mmol/L or higher fasting, or 7.8 mmol/L or higher at any time, see a doctor for a proper blood test. These are the cut-offs in Malaysia’s Clinical Practice Guidelines (2020), for blood taken from a vein: Test Normal Prediabetes Diabetes HbA1c Below 5.7% 5.7% to 6.2% 6.3% or above Fasting glucose Below 6.1 mmol/L 6.1 to 6.9 mmol/L 7.0 mmol/L or above 2 hours after glucose drink (OGTT) Below 7.8 mmol/L 7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L 11.1 mmol/L or above Random glucose — — 11.1 mmol/L or above, with symptoms Malaysia uses an HbA1c of 6.3% to diagnose diabetes, lower than the 6.5% used in many countries. Local research found 6.5% would miss too many Malaysians with diabetes. If you have no symptoms , diabetes is diagnosed only after two abnormal results , either two different tests on the same blood sample or the same test on two occasions. One abnormal result is enough if you also have symptoms such as thirst, passing a lot of urine, or weight loss. Prediabetes means your blood sugar is higher than normal but not yet in the diabetes range. This is where early action works best. In a large US trial, a lifestyle programme cut the number of people with prediabetes who went on to develop type 2 diabetes by 58% , and by 71% in people over 60. Malaysian guidelines recommend: Losing at least 7% of your body weight if you are overweight. For a 75 kg person, that is about 5 kg. At least 150 minutes of activity a week , such as brisk walking for 30 minutes on five days. Cutting sweet drinks and refined carbohydrates. Fill half your plate with vegetables, a quarter with protein and a quarter with whole grains, following the Suku-Suku Separuh guide. A blood sugar test every year. Your doctor may also suggest medicine if your risk is high. Thirty minutes of brisk walking on five days a week meets the activity target for preventing diabetes. Klinik Kesihatan: government health clinics offer free blood sugar, blood pressure, BMI and cholesterol checks under the National Health Screening Initiative. Book in the MySejahtera app under Appointments, then NHSI. Your results appear in the app. More than 2.65 million people have been screened since 2022. PeKa B40: free screening, including blood sugar, for Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah recipients aged 40 and above, and their spouses. Check your eligibility with your IC number on the PeKa B40 website. PERKESO Health Screening Programme: a free, one-time screening for PERKESO contributors aged 40 to 59, booked through the SEHATi app. Diabetes Malaysia’s KL event: Diabetes Malaysia lists a World Diabetes Day state event in Kuala Lumpur on Saturday 14 November, 9am to 4pm . The venue had not been announced at the time of writing. Call Diabetes Malaysia on 03-7957 4062 for details. For more on these programmes, see free health screening in Malaysia 2026 . Any GP clinic can also do an HbA1c or fasting glucose test. Very high blood sugar can cause diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) or a hyperosmolar state (HHS). Both are medical emergencies, and they are sometimes the first sign of undiagnosed diabetes, especially in older people. Go to an emergency department or call 999 if someone has Vomiting or stomach pain with high blood sugar Fast or deep breathing, or a fast heartbeat Fruity-smelling breath Drowsiness or confusion Extreme thirst and passing a lot of urine, with weakness Don’t drive yourself. See our guide to clinic or emergency department . When is World Diabetes Day 2026? Saturday 14 November 2026. The theme for 2026 and 2027 is “Early action on diabetes”. What HbA1c level means diabetes in Malaysia? An HbA1c of 6.3% or above, confirmed by a second abnormal result if you have no symptoms. An HbA1c of 5.7% to 6.2% is prediabetes. Do I need to fast for a diabetes test? Not for an HbA1c test. For a fasting glucose test or an oral glucose tolerance test, fast for at least 8 hours beforehand. Plain water is fine. Can a glucometer diagnose diabetes? No. A finger-prick reading is a first screen only. If it is high, a doctor will confirm with a blood test from a vein, such as fasting glucose, HbA1c or an OGTT. Where can I get a free diabetes test in KL? At government health clinics (book through MySejahtera under NHSI), through PeKa B40 if you are an STR recipient aged 40+, or through PERKESO’s screening programme if you are a contributor aged 40–59. Can prediabetes be reversed? Often, yes. Losing at least 7% of body weight and doing 150 minutes of activity a week can bring blood sugar back to normal and greatly lowers the risk of type 2 diabetes.

title: Free health screening in Malaysia 2026: PERKESO, PeKa B40, Selangor Saring and more
desc: Several free health screening programmes run in Malaysia in 2026. Who qualifies for each, what they test, how to book, and which checks you need at your age.
headings: Why get screened if you feel fine? · Free screening programmes at a glance · PERKESO Health Screening Programme (HSP 2026) · PeKa B40 (for STR recipients aged 40+) · Free checks at government health clinics · Selangor Saring 2026 · What Budget 2027 changes · Which screenings you need at your age · How to prepare, and what to do with your results
keywords: Prevention Free health screening in Malaysia kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october kesihatan mental depression anxiety stress kemurungan mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp saringan check-up checkup medical
body: PERKESO’s Health Screening Programme (HSP 2026) is free, once only, for Malaysian workers aged 40–59 who meet the contribution rules. Check and book in the SEHATi app. PeKa B40 is free for Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR) recipients aged 40 and above, and their spouses. No registration is needed. Government health clinics (Klinik Kesihatan) offer free basic checks for blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol, BMI and mental health. Selangor Saring runs free community screening days across the state until December. Register in the SELangkah app. Budget 2027 keeps PeKa B40 going and adds PERKESO screening vouchers for commercial vehicle drivers. High blood pressure, diabetes and high cholesterol usually cause no symptoms for years. By the time they do, they may already have damaged the heart, kidneys or eyes. Screening finds them early, when they are easier to treat. Recent Malaysian figures show how common hidden problems are. Among PERKESO contributors screened between 2023 and 2025, mostly aged 40–59, 59.2% were overweight or obese , about 19% had diabetes and 17.45% had high blood pressure. In PeKa B40’s 2025 screening, 44.37% of participants had diabetes, high blood pressure or high cholesterol. Blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol checks are part of every free screening programme below. Programme Who it is for How to book PERKESO HSP 2026 Malaysian workers aged 40–59 who meet PERKESO’s contribution rules, once only SEHATi app, then a panel clinic PeKa B40 STR recipients aged 40+, and their spouses Automatic; go to a PeKa B40 clinic with your MyKad Klinik Kesihatan (NHSI) Everyone; free basic checks Walk in, or book through MySejahtera Selangor Saring Selangor residents SELangkah app; sessions until December Rules can change during the year, so check the official app or website for each programme before you go. PERKESO (SOCSO) offers a free health screening to working Malaysians. The current edition, listed as HSP 2026 in PERKESO’s SEHATi help pages, continues the HSP 3.0 programme that began in 2023. Who qualifies: Malaysian citizens aged 40 to 59 At least one month of Invalidity Scheme (Skim Keilatan) contributions in the current year, and at least 12 months of contributions in total You have not had an HSP screening before . It is a one-time benefit, not a yearly one. What is tested in 2026: a physical examination and family history, full blood count, HbA1c (average blood sugar), a fasting cholesterol profile, a urine test and a mental health screening, followed by a review of your results with a doctor. Women are also offered a Pap smear and a mammogram. For a small extra charge you can add blood group, liver and kidney tests. How to book: download the SEHATi app, check your eligibility and choose a panel clinic. The clinic will confirm your eligibility with your IC number. If you are not eligible, SEHATi also lists paid screening packages for PERKESO contributors. PERKESO has not published a closing date for 2026, so check the SEHATi app for the latest details. PeKa B40 is a government scheme run by ProtectHealth for lower-income Malaysians. You qualify if you are a Malaysian aged 40 or above and receive Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR) , or are the spouse of a recipient. Eligibility is automatic, so there is nothing to register. See our PeKa B40 guide for how to check and the full list of benefits. The free screening covers your health history and risk factors, a physical examination, blood and urine tests, a mental health screening, and a breast examination for women or a prostate examination for men at risk. It is done at private GP clinics registered with PeKa B40. You can check your eligibility with your IC number on the PeKa B40 website. Since 2019 the scheme has served more than 1.9 million people. Budget 2027 allocates RM80 million to continue it. Under the National Health Screening Initiative (NHSI), government health clinics and PeKa B40 clinics offer free basic screening for blood sugar, blood pressure, BMI, cholesterol and mental health . If a result is abnormal, you are referred for confirmatory tests and follow-up. You can walk in to your nearest Klinik Kesihatan or book an appointment through the MySejahtera app. Government clinics also run other free or low-cost screenings, such as cervical screening and mammogram referrals for women. See our guide to breast cancer screening and free mammograms . Selangor Saring is the Selangor state government’s free health screening programme, run with Selcare since 2022. In 2026 it has RM2.5 million in funding and runs from January to December , mostly at weekends, across the state’s 56 constituencies. Depending on your risk, tests at the screening days can include heart, blood pressure, diabetes and kidney checks, screening for breast, cervical, colorectal and prostate cancer, and eye, dental and hearing checks. How to register: fill in the screening form in the SELangkah app, then choose a location and date. Some sessions accept walk-ins, but booking first is safer. The Selcare helpline is 1-800-22-6600. Budget 2027, tabled on 9 October 2026, includes several screening measures: PeKa B40 continues , with RM80 million for free screening and treatment support for STR recipients and their spouses aged 40+. Screening vouchers for commercial vehicle drivers , worth up to RM30, through PERKESO. Free thalassaemia screening at MOH facilities extended to the husbands and children of families who carry the gene. Screening and mobile clinics run by university teaching hospitals for rural and lower-income communities. Malaysia’s Ministry of Health Clinical Practice Guidelines recommend these checks for adults at average risk. Your doctor may advise earlier or more frequent tests if you have risk factors or a family history. Check Who and how often Blood pressure All adults over 18, at least once a year Blood sugar (diabetes) From age 30, yearly if normal. Earlier if you are overweight and have another risk factor, or had diabetes in pregnancy Cholesterol All adults over 30. From 18 if you are at high risk, for example with a strong family history Cervical screening Women aged 30–49: HPV test, every 5 years if negative. Pap smear at ages 21–29 and 50–65 Breast (mammogram) Every 2 years for women aged 50–74. Earlier for women at high risk Bowel (colorectal) Ages 50–75: a stool test (iFOBT) every year, with colonoscopy if positive Ask whether you need to fast. If your tests include a fasting blood test, you will usually be asked not to eat for 8 to 10 hours beforehand. Plain water is fine. Bring your MyKad, a list of any medicines you take, and any previous results. Don’t skip the results review. A screening only helps if abnormal results are followed up. If a result is borderline or high, ask what the next step is and when to repeat the test. Screening is not for symptoms If you already have symptoms, such as chest pain, unexplained weight loss, a breast lump or blood in your stool, see a doctor now rather than waiting for a screening day. For chest pain or difficulty breathing, call 999. Who is eligible for the free PERKESO health screening in 2026? Malaysian citizens aged 40 to 59 with at least one month of Invalidity Scheme contributions this year, at least 12 months in total, and no previous HSP screening. Check your eligibility in the SEHATi app. Can I do the PERKESO health screening every year? No. The HSP is a one-time benefit. If you have already had an HSP screening, PERKESO contributors can book paid packages through the SEHATi app instead. How do I know if I qualify for PeKa B40? If you are a Malaysian aged 40 or above and receive Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR), or are the spouse of a recipient, you qualify automatically. You can check with your IC number on the PeKa B40 website. Is health screening free at Klinik Kesihatan? Yes, basic screening for blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol, BMI and mental health is free at government health clinics under the National Health Screening Initiative. You can book through MySejahtera. How do I register for Selangor Saring? Fill in the screening form in the SELangkah app and choose a location and date. Sessions run across Selangor until December 2026, mostly at weekends.

title: Dengue vaccine in Malaysia: what Qdenga can and can’t do
desc: With dengue cases up sharply in 2026, many people are asking about the vaccine. Who can get it, how well it works, the important DENV-3 caveat, and what it costs.
headings: Dengue in Malaysia in 2026 · What is the dengue vaccine? · Who can have it, and who should not · How well does it work? · The DENV-3 caveat · Side effects · Cost and where to get it · Keep preventing bites, even if vaccinated
keywords: Prevention Dengue vaccine in Malaysia Dengue Denggi denggi aedes nyamuk mosquito kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal vaksin suntikan jab immunisation klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Qdenga is the only dengue vaccine available in Malaysia. It is conditionally registered for people aged 4 and above, given as two doses three months apart. It is not part of the National Immunisation Programme, so it is only available at private clinics and hospitals. In trials it cut dengue hospitalisations by about 84% over four and a half years. In people who have never had dengue, it did not protect against DENV-3, the strain driving Malaysia’s 2026 surge. Discuss this with your doctor. The vaccine does not replace mosquito control or knowing the warning signs of severe dengue. Malaysia recorded 78,225 dengue cases and 68 deaths between 4 January and 25 October 2026, according to the national iDengue portal. Selangor accounts for the largest share, followed by the Federal Territories and Johor. By early September, cases were 66% higher than in the same period of 2025, and deaths had almost doubled. The Ministry of Health has linked the rise to a shift in the dominant dengue strain, from DENV-2 to DENV-3 . That matters when thinking about the vaccine, as explained below. Dengue is spread by Aedes mosquitoes, which bite mostly in the early morning and late afternoon. Qdenga (also known as TAK-003) is a live, weakened vaccine designed to protect against all four types of dengue virus (DENV-1 to DENV-4). It is given as an injection under the skin, in two doses three months apart . A booster dose is not currently part of the approved schedule. Malaysia’s Drug Control Authority gave it conditional registration in February 2024 . That means the company must keep submitting safety and effectiveness data. A renewal of the conditional registration has been reported from February 2026. The vaccine is not in the National Immunisation Programme . In August 2026, the Health Minister said the Ministry was still studying whether to include it, including a cost-benefit analysis. For now, it is only offered privately. In Malaysia, it is registered for people aged 4 and above , whether or not they have had dengue before. There is little data for people over 60. The World Health Organization recommends it mainly for children aged 6 to 16 in areas with high dengue transmission, and says people up to 60 with conditions such as diabetes or high blood pressure may also be offered it. You should not have it if you: are pregnant or breastfeeding (and you should avoid becoming pregnant for at least a month afterwards) have a weakened immune system, for example from chemotherapy, high-dose steroids or HIV with low immunity had a severe allergic reaction to a previous dose or to any ingredient If you have a high fever on the day, the vaccination should be delayed. The main trial followed about 20,000 children aged 4 to 16 in Asia and Latin America. Four and a half years after the second dose, the vaccine had reduced: Group Fewer dengue cases Fewer hospital admissions Everyone 61% 84% Had dengue before 64% 86% Never had dengue 54% 79% Protection was highest in the first year and a half, and lowest in children aged 4 to 5. Protection was not the same against every dengue type. In people who had never had dengue , the trial found good protection against DENV-2 and some against DENV-1, but no protection against DENV-3 , and too few DENV-4 cases to show any benefit. The few cases of severe dengue in vaccinated people who had never had dengue were all DENV-3. The difference was not statistically significant, but WHO says a higher risk “cannot be conclusively ruled out”.
